for baseline in (.8, .08):
    disparity = 28*baseline/4
    estimates = [28*baseline/(disparity+e) for e in (-.5, 0, .5)]
    print(f"b = {baseline:.2f} m, d = {disparity:.2f} px   z =", np.round(estimates, 3))

## One actual update from image error

Each camera has its own mean squared RGB difference from lesson 6, $L_A$ or $L_B$. For a single view the denominator counts $33\cdot33\cdot3=3267$ values. Initially $L_A$ is zero to numerical precision and $L_B\approx0.00468808$. With equal weight for the cameras, $L=(L_A+L_B)/2\approx0.00234404$. The held-out view never enters this sum.

There is a single unknown $z$. To check the derivative, we render two neighboring cases, $z-h$ and $z+h$, with $h=0.002$ world units. The denominator of the slope is the distance between these cases, $2h=0.004$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
g &\approx \frac{L(2.402)-L(2.398)}{0.004}\\
  &\approx (0.0023357144-0.0023523820)/0.004=-0.004167.
\end{aligned}
$$

The minus sign says that increasing depth a little decreases the loss here. With a learning rate of $\eta=80$ we get $z_{\rm new}=2.4-80(-0.004167)\approx2.73335$. The rate converts slope into a change in depth; the value 80 belongs to this particular loss scale. Depth stays within 1.25 to 7 to keep the model in front of the camera. After twenty updates $z\approx3.8101$. The held-out error falls from $0.00277686$ to $0.00001703$. Training on A alone leaves the loss curve essentially flat.

fig = demo.ray_landscape("en")
display(fig)
plt.close(fig)

z = 2.4
for step in range(20):
    z, gradient = sr.depth_step(z, (0,.8))
print(round(z, 6), sr.ray_loss(z, (0,.8)), sr.ray_loss(z, (-.6,)))
assert sr.ray_loss(z, (-.6,)) < sr.ray_loss(2.4, (-.6,))

## How a single pixel votes

So far the slope of the loss has appeared as one number from two nearby renders. We can look inside that number. Camera B, row 15, column 14. The target has an orange center there while the closer model shows a lighter edge. Blue is a revealing channel since it drops sharply on the way from white to orange. The model gives $I=0.66766$, the target $Y=0.20773$. Both range from zero to one. The residual is $r=I-Y=+0.45993$. The plus sign means excess blue. Its square adds about $0.21154$ to the image sum before division by the number of samples.

Depth increases slightly. The model center shifts right, and a denser part of the footprint moves over our pixel. Renders at 2.398 and 2.402 m measure the change in intensity. Blue would fall by about $0.50675$ per meter **if** the local slope persisted that far. The measurement itself spans just four millimeters. The slope times a small depth displacement gives the intensity change. Another multiplication by $2r$ gives the change in squared error. The 2 comes from expanding $(r+\delta)^2-r^2=2r\delta+\delta^2$. After division by a small $\delta$, the second term goes to zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{\rm pixel}&=\frac{2(I-Y)}{3267}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta z}\\
&\approx\frac{2\cdot0.45993}{3267}\cdot(-0.50675)
\approx-0.00014268.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the vote of one channel at one pixel in the derivative of B's mean error with respect to depth. Neighboring pixels can vote the other way. Blue at column 10 of the same row is already too dark. More darkening there makes the match worse, producing a positive contribution of about $+0.00002545$. The map below adds the three **signed** votes at each location. Faraway white background says almost nothing about depth. Strong votes appear where sliding the silhouette changes the color. Adding up camera B gives about $-0.008334$. Averaging across the two training cameras recovers $-0.004167$ because A contributes zero along this family of models.

The code includes another check. The same frame is rendered from tensors. The chain from depth to every color stays inside PyTorch, including the change of scale and the projection. A backward pass combines contributions from all the channels using differentiation rules. These independent calculations measure the same slope. Their last digits can differ because the first one uses a finite step.

from splat_fit import render_parallel
import torch

cam_b = sr.translated_camera(.8)
def frame_at(z):
    return sr.render_scene(sr.ray_scene(z), cam_b, 33, 33)

prediction, target = frame_at(2.4), frame_at(4)
h = .002
slope = (frame_at(2.4+h)-frame_at(2.4-h))/(2*h)
votes = 2*(prediction-target)*slope/prediction.size
print("B[15,14,blue]:", round(votes[15,14,2], 8), "  B total:", round(votes.sum(), 8))

z = torch.tensor(2.4, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
centers = z*z.new_tensor([[.10,-.05,1.]])
scales = z*z.new_tensor([[.12,.08,.06]])
tensor_frame = render_parallel(centers, scales, z.new_tensor([[.85,.2,.08]]),
                               z.new_tensor([.9]), .8)
(tensor_frame-torch.as_tensor(target)).square().mean().backward()
print("PyTorch:", round(z.grad.item(), 8))
np.testing.assert_allclose(votes.sum(), z.grad.item(), rtol=2e-5)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3.2), constrained_layout=True)
axes[0].imshow(prediction); axes[1].imshow(target)
signed = votes.sum(axis=2)
limit = np.abs(signed).max()
axes[2].imshow(signed, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-limit, vmax=limit)
titles = (["Модель B", "Образец B", "Синий −, красный +"] if lang=="ru"
          else ["B prediction", "B target", "Blue −, red +"])
for ax, title in zip(axes, titles):
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("u (px)"); ax.set_ylabel("v (px)")
    ax.plot(14,15,"+",color="black",ms=10)
plt.show()

## From one parameter to a scene with two Gaussians

Now we untie position from width. In a separate experiment two splats have independent centers and RGB values, six numbers each. Their scales, rotations, opacities, and camera calibration are known. Two color images come from cameras at $X=-0.8$ and $+0.65$. A third camera at $+0.12$ supplies a check view. All three panels below use that camera.

The program computes footprints, blends them and averages errors over **only the first two** frames. In PyTorch a computation graph connects color and center to every rendered pixel. Calling `backward()` gives each of the 12 numbers the rate of change of the shared loss, as in lesson 8. Adam chooses the steps here. It keeps running estimates of each parameter's gradient and squared gradient to adjust the size of its update. The sorted layer indices stay fixed within a step; an order swap itself is discrete. After an update RGB stays within zero to one and depth within 1.25 to 7.

Training starts with inaccurate centers and muted colors. Across 45 steps the held-out MSE drops from about $0.002427$ to $0.00000827$. Low error on another image checks the prediction at that particular view. Hidden details and unobserved sides still have no measurements.

import torch
from splat_fit import train_two_splats
torch.set_num_threads(1)
run = train_two_splats(45)
print(np.array(run["history"])[[0, 15, 45]])
assert run["history"][-1][1] < run["history"][0][1] / 100

fig = demo.panel([run["target"],run["before"],run["after"]], ["Held-out view","Before","After"])
display(fig)
plt.close(fig)

### What changed in the second fit?

The pair of splats now has twelve controls in place of one. Each center has three numbers in meters. Each color has three unitless fractions. An identical numerical gradient for color and depth would describe different changes. The optimizer receives a separate array for each kind and keeps an update history for each element. The observations have a shape too. Two frames with 33 rows, 33 columns and three channels contain $2\cdot33\cdot33\cdot3=6534$ numbers. This need not amount to 6534 independent geometric equations. Thousands of neighboring values may describe the same white background.

The first fit had no choice between altering color and altering coverage. The second one does. A model painting excess color on a patch of white can reduce error by moving that patch back toward the object. It could also move its color closer to white. Then it would match the background better but leave a pale patch inside the silhouette. Other pixels and the second camera carry that cost into the objective. There are two clues in the “Before” image. A displaced contour points toward geometry. An error that remains where the contours already agree can also come from color or opacity.

Here we synthesized all three images and therefore know the answer. With photographs, true 3D centers are unavailable. A reserved camera gives a way to evaluate the prediction. If its score were used after every update to choose the best settings, it would participate in that choice. An independent final assessment would then need another photograph. Our step count was fixed in advance and the held-out curve is merely recorded. The next experiment introduces a different reason why error might persist. Even with accurate cameras and perfectly clean backgrounds, one splat may have too few peaks to represent two separate details.

## Experiments and worked answers

Would a second photograph from precisely the same position help once the first view matches? How distinguishable are the depths with a very small baseline?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

A duplicate of A doubles the number of measurements and the denominator of the average, leaving the same flat dependence on depth. With $b=0.008$ instead of $0.8$, the center discrepancy between the 2.4 and 4 hypotheses is only $3.733/100\approx0.037$ pixels. A difference still exists in theory. In photographs it is easier to lose to noise, blur, and pose error.

</details>

### A larger canvas

A white border is added to both images with the original pixels and projections left intact. There are now twice as many color samples. Prediction and target agree throughout the added region. What happens to MSE and to the first depth update with the same learning rate?

<details><summary>The border calculation</summary>

The numerator gains a sum of zeros. The denominator doubles, so the loss and its derivative halve. At the old rate of 80 the depth displacement is about $0.33335/2=0.16668$ m. The original patch still contains the same geometric information. The normalization that translates it into an update length has changed. The added values must agree at neighboring depth settings too, or the border's contribution to the derivative must be included.

</details>

### The camera is on the wrong side

The mark has $u_A=18.8$ and $u_B=13.2$. A camera file lists $b=-0.8$ m. What depth comes out of the two marks? How does it fit the requirement $z>0$?

<details><summary>Checking the sign of the baseline</summary>

The difference is $18.8-13.2=+5.6$ pixels. The numerator is $28(-0.8)=-22.4$, giving $-22.4/5.6=-4$ m. Our camera looks forward along positive Z. A positive depth cannot match both marks with that sign for the baseline. Checking the translation direction and the order of image subtraction comes before adjusting the learning rate. Exchanging both cameras would flip the signs of both the baseline and the disparity, preserving the original result.

</details>

### Whose gradient is it?

One camera gives a depth slope of $+0.002$, the other $-0.008$. The images have equal size and the cameras have equal weights. Where does depth move at a learning rate of 10? What if the second camera accidentally gets weight zero?

<details><summary>Combining two votes</summary>

Equal weights give $(0.002-0.008)/2=-0.003$. Descent subtracts the slope, increasing depth by $0.03$ m. If the mean is taken only over the first camera, its slope is $+0.002$ and depth falls by $0.02$ m. Two views can disagree on the direction to move. The sign of each contribution depends on what happens to that particular image as the candidate model shifts.

</details>

title: Lesson 17. When one splat cannot do the job

cells.source: The target has two blue beads with a pale gap between them. The model has a single broad splat and an almost transparent speck off to the side. We can move the broad splat or fade it. Its horizontal slice still has one peak where the target has two. Sometimes the next useful move is a change to the list of Gaussians itself.

## One starting point, several possible moves

The camera, color, and background stay fixed. The target is on the left, the model on the right. Separate operations can copy a selected splat, replace it with two children, remove faint splats, or reduce all opacities together. Returning to the starting scene lets us compare these moves from a common reference. An ordinary gradient step moves centers horizontally and changes their opacity.

Each comparison has three different readings. MSE measures color discrepancies across 33 × 33 pixels. Splat count measures the length of the list. The byte count includes just the numerical scene parameters stored in float32. An edit that takes more space and makes the image worse is an informative outcome too.

A square on both images marks the sampled pixel. The column slider moves it along row 16. It starts in the gap, where the red-channel difference is about −0.463.
display(demo.experiment(17, "en"))

## A white gap belongs in the middle

The previous fit began with a useful clue. Even its poor initial model already had the right number of objects. Here the number of independently movable details is itself unknown. From across the room a blue cloud might look fairly similar to two beads. A horizontal scan through both centers gives us three specific locations for comparing colors.

The camera center is at zero and its focal length is 42 pixels. Both target centers have depth 4 m, at $X=-0.54$ and $X=0.42$ m. Their projected centers fall at columns $16+42(-0.54)/4=10.33$ and $16+42(0.42)/4=20.41$. Both have $Y=0$, so row 16 passes through them. Columns 10, 16 and 20 serve three different purposes. The first and last fall near bead centers. The middle one lands in the gap. In NumPy the indexing order is row, column, channel. For instance, `image[16, 10, 0]` is red intensity in the left bead. Red intensity on the white background is one. Blue paint takes away a lot of red, so each bead appears as a **valley** in a graph of the red channel.

| Red channel on row 16 | Left center | Gap | Right center |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Two target beads | 0.215 | 0.806 | 0.219 |
| Initial model | 0.453 | 0.344 | 0.531 |

The left and right parts need to get darker while the middle needs to get lighter. The middle of the broad splat is currently its darkest part. Increasing opacity everywhere would darken both ends while worsening the gap. Pulling the whole splat to the right would pay for an improvement on one bead with a mistake on the other. The three numbers reveal the **shape** of the error more clearly than one average. The figure keeps the entire row. The three marked columns help read the profiles even where the lines nearly overlap.

camera = sr.translated_camera(0, focal=42)
start = sr.density_scene()
cases = [sr.density_scene(True), start, sr.density_edit(start, "split"), sr.density_edit(start, "clone")]
names = (["Образец", "До", "Два ребёнка", "Клон"] if lang == "ru"
         else ["Target", "Before", "Two children", "Clone"])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.3), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, indices in zip(axes, [(0, 1, 2), (0, 1, 3)]):
    for i in indices:
        image = sr.render_scene(cases[i], camera, 33, 33)
        ax.plot(image[16, :, 0], ["k-", "C0--", "C1-", "C2-"][i], label=names[i])
    for u in [10, 16, 20]:
        ax.axvline(u,color=".7",lw=.7)
    ax.set(xlabel="u (px)", ylabel="R", ylim=(0,1.05)); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

## A step inside the list

Initially the list holds two splats. The broad one has $x=-0.16$, horizontal scale $s_x=0.63$, and center opacity $o=0.77$. A small shift changes the frame's RGB and its error. For the two derivatives we take two neighboring measurements apiece, starting each from the same original state as in the previous lesson. We get $g_x\approx-0.00304635$ MSE per unit of length and $g_o\approx0.00834045$ per unit of opacity.

At learning rate $\eta=3$, the new coordinate is $x'=-0.16-3(-0.00304635)\approx-0.15086$. The new opacity is $o'=0.77-3(0.00834045)\approx0.74498$. The splat moves right and becomes a touch paler on white. The small splat gets its own two derivatives. After the simultaneous update MSE falls from $0.00467723$ to $0.00446188$. Indices 0 and 1 still refer to the same two splats. The gradient of a value in row 0 cannot create row 2.

initial = sr.density_scene()
print(np.round(sr.density_gradients(initial), 7))
updated = sr.density_step(initial)
print(updated["splats"][0]["center"], updated["splats"][0]["opacity"])
assert len(initial["splats"]) == len(updated["splats"]) == 2
assert sr.density_loss(updated) < sr.density_loss(initial)

### Can another center update solve it?

This is an easy place to misdiagnose the fit. MSE went down after the first step. Does that guarantee a white gap after enough steps? The size of the first improvement cannot tell us. Our experiment only allows a horizontal center and an opacity update for each splat. Its scales stay fixed. Both center gradients and both opacity gradients are measured **before** editing any row. Otherwise the next derivative would see a different scene and the collection of gradients would no longer describe the same starting image.

The broad splat's opacity derivative is about 0.00834 per unit of $o$. A small opacity increase of 0.001 would therefore raise error by about $0.00834\cdot0.001=0.00000834$. A decrease in $o$ helps on average even though the left bead currently needs more blue. It is a compromise over all pixels, including the background. After twelve ordinary steps the same model's error is about 0.004002. Parameter motion helped. The shapes a single wide bell can take remain limited.

The second, tiny splat deserves a closer look too. Technically it already supplies a second peak. It starts almost transparent and well above the two beads. The only available center movement is horizontal, so it cannot drop onto their row. Its initial horizontal gradient is almost seventy times weaker than the big splat's. Free vertical movement, independent scales and a different initialization would change the problem. This particular run can teach us how the operations work. It would be odd to conclude that two freely adjustable Gaussians cannot represent two beads at all. Two Gaussians are precisely what made the target.

## A clone darkens the image. A split changes its shape

A **clone** appends a copy of the center, shape, color, and opacity. At the original splat center $\alpha=0.77$, so $1-0.77=0.23$ of the background passed through. Two identical layers pass $0.23\cdot0.23=0.0529$, making their combined opacity $1-0.0529=0.9471$. Identical coordinates therefore change the image. The oversized dark blue region raises MSE to $0.01214659$. Future steps can move the two copies independently.

A **split** removes the broad parent and inserts two children. For a repeatable example we place them symmetrically along the horizontal axis. Their offset is $0.65\cdot0.63=0.4095$, giving centers $-0.16-0.4095=-0.5695$ and $-0.16+0.4095=0.2495$. Each of their three scales is divided by $1.6$. For instance the horizontal one becomes $0.63/1.6=0.39375$. They inherit the parent's color and $o$. Two peaks begin to emerge and MSE becomes $0.00347211$. For a different target or starting splat this same operation can make the image worse.

Both edits grew the list from two rows to three. After cloning it contains the parent and its exact copy. After splitting the parent is gone, leaving two displaced splats and the original speck.

fig = demo.density_chart("en")
display(fig)
plt.close(fig)

### Can opacity be shared without a jump?

Two original-strength copies cut off most of the background. A tempting alternative is to give each one half the old opacity. At the center this means $0.77/2=0.385$. The remaining background becomes $(1-0.385)^2=0.378225$, versus 0.23 before the copy. Translucent layers also occlude one another. Halving one number does not preserve the final color.

At the center of coincident splats we can work backward. The two equal layers should leave exactly the old transmittance $T=0.23$. With $a$ denoting the new opacity of each layer, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1-a)(1-a)&=0.23,\\
1-a&=\sqrt{0.23}\approx0.47958,\\
a&=1-0.47958\approx0.52042.
\end{aligned}
$$

The positive root follows from transmittance being a fraction between zero and one. This might seem to finish the calculation. But the center is just one address. At a distance where the Gaussian weight falls to one half, the old model gives $\alpha=0.77\cdot0.5=0.385$. The two layers together now cover $1-(1-0.52042\cdot0.5)^2\approx0.4527$. Their edges are still darker, even though the center has been matched exactly. Even careful duplication alters the profile before the optimizer makes another step.

The difference came from multiplying two transmittances. There is no constant opacity adjustment that reproduces the old soft footprint everywhere while keeping two identical child shapes. A split also changes centers and scales. Immediately after a split, red in the gap still sits near 0.357 versus 0.806 in the target. Now the two children have independent directions in which to move. What changed is the ability of **subsequent** steps to improve the shape, something that shows up only once fitting resumes.

parent_o = .77
child_o = 1 - np.sqrt(1-parent_o)
for w in (1, .5, .1, 0):
    old = parent_o*w
    pair = 1 - (1-child_o*w)**2
    print(f"w={w:.1f}   old={old:.5f}   pair={pair:.5f}   Δ={pair-old:+.5f}")

## Pruning and resetting have different effects

**Pruning** removes a splat altogether. Our threshold $0.03$ applies to center opacity. The speck has $o=0.015<0.03$, so it disappears. The large splat remains useful. The list shrinks and the error stays close to its initial value, at $0.00467882$. It actually **increased** slightly. A tiny contribution still has an effect.

An **opacity reset** leaves centers and shapes in place. The new value $o'=\min(o,0.01)$ is the smaller of the old $o$ and one hundredth. For instance $0.77$ becomes $0.01$, whereas $0.004$ stays $0.004$. When the splats are faint, more light passes through and a hidden layer has a chance to contribute. Optimization can build useful opacities back up. Immediately after resetting, the image is almost white and MSE is $0.01592582$. Applying the pruning threshold of $0.03$ at this moment would remove every splat. Both order and timing matter in a full training run.

for action in ("clone","split","prune","reset"):
    scene = sr.density_edit(initial, action)
    n = len(scene["splats"])
    print(f"{action:6s} N={n}, bytes={56*n}, MSE={sr.density_loss(scene):.8f}")
assert len(sr.density_edit(sr.density_edit(initial, "reset"), "prune")["splats"]) == 0
cells.output:
clone  N=3, bytes=168, MSE=0.01214659
split  N=3, bytes=168, MSE=0.00347211
prune  N=1, bytes=56, MSE=0.00467882
reset  N=2, bytes=112, MSE=0.01592582

cells.source:
### Pruning seen by a different camera

The crumb has opacity 0.015. Even at its own center it receives at most that fraction of the color. If a foreground layer leaves only one tenth of the light, its pixel weight is at most $0.1\cdot0.015=0.0015$. This gives a reason to test removal, but it does not tell us its cost for the **whole image**. A large faint splat touches many pixels. A small one might sit on a thin high-contrast detail. A new camera position can also reveal a footprint that used to hide behind a nearer layer.

We can compare the original, an immediate clone, an immediate split and a removal at two camera positions. The bead geometry is known, so each target view can be produced independently. The edits were chosen from the frontal image. Our second camera moves to $+0.6$ m with the same focal length and orientation. It checks a decision and never contributes to the gradients. With pruning, frontal error rises from about 0.00467723 to 0.00467882. At the other camera it goes from 0.00420203 to 0.00420206. Rounding to three decimals would hide the difference entirely. The two scenes still differ and one splat's parameter cost really did go away.

Another legitimate choice is to include storage in the decision. Suppose we add a charge $\lambda N$ to MSE when selecting a scene. Here $N$ is the integer splat count and $\lambda$ is a charge measured in units of mean error per additional row. This gives a score $J=L+\lambda N$. It does not create any new pixel. It defines what “better” means for this particular comparison. An immediate split gains $0.00467723-0.00347211=0.00120512$ in MSE at the cost of one extra row. A charge of 0.0005 leaves a net advantage for the split. At a charge of 0.002 the original model wins. This calculation compares two completed states. A budget of twelve more training steps calls for a fresh comparison after those steps.

The original work changes density using an accumulated signal and rules for size and opacity. Here the row charge serves only to make our choice explicit. The derivative of $J$ with respect to a coordinate at a fixed row count equals the derivative of $L$. Adding the constant $\lambda N$ gives the existing center no direction in which to create a neighbor.

held_camera = sr.translated_camera(.6, focal=42)
held_target = sr.render_scene(sr.density_scene(True), held_camera, 33, 33)
for action in ("unchanged", "clone", "split", "prune", "reset"):
    candidate = initial if action == "unchanged" else sr.density_edit(initial, action)
    held_frame = sr.render_scene(candidate, held_camera, 33, 33)
    held_mse = np.mean((held_frame-held_target)**2)
    before_loss = sr.density_loss(candidate)
    fitted = candidate
    for _ in range(12):
        fitted = sr.density_step(fitted)
    print(f"{action:9} N={len(candidate['splats'])}  train={before_loss:.8f}  "
          f"held={held_mse:.8f}  train@12={sr.density_loss(fitted):.8f}")

## How a training loop makes the decision

In one adaptive pass of the experiment we first compute all gradients in the old scene. Any splat with $o<0.03$ is marked for removal. For the others we compare the magnitude of their horizontal gradient with $0.001$. For the broad splat $|-0.00304635|>0.001$. This flags an area where moving the center can appreciably change the loss. It measures sensitivity to a shift, with no guarantee that this is where a detail is missing.

Now we need a copy or two children. In this experiment a horizontal scale above $0.32$ counts as broad. Since $0.63>0.32$, the splat is split. A sufficiently narrow one with the same strong signal would be cloned. A budget of 16 splats keeps each step easy to inspect. After the first adaptive pass the broad splat has become two and the faint speck is gone, so the count is two again. The MSE is different, about $0.00348773$. A splat counter alone would miss this restructuring.

The original 3DGS implementation accumulates a signal for **visible** splats over training steps. It takes lengths of the two-component screen-center gradients and averages them over observations. Size is compared with scene extent. A split samples children around the parent's center using its shape and orientation. The code can also prune excessively large footprints. Our single-camera version uses the derivative along the world x axis, deterministic child offsets, and explicit controls. The example thresholds belong to its particular coordinates and loss. [Algorithm in the paper](https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/) and [parameter operations in the reference implementation](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting/blob/main/scene/gaussian_model.py).

adaptive = sr.density_pass(initial)
print([(s["center"][0],s["scales"][0],s["opacity"]) for s in adaptive["splats"]])
assert len(adaptive["splats"]) == len(initial["splats"])
assert sr.density_loss(adaptive) < sr.density_loss(initial)
for _ in range(8):
    adaptive = sr.density_step(adaptive)
print("8 steps:", sr.density_loss(adaptive))

fig = demo.density_figure("en", operation="adaptive", steps=8)
display(fig)
plt.close(fig)

## Experiments and worked answers

How much memory did a clone add? Why can the change in total GPU memory use not be read directly from that number?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

A splat stores three coordinates, three scales, four quaternion components, three color channels, and an opacity. That is $3+3+4+3+1=14$ numbers. One float32 occupies $32/8=4$ bytes. A clone adds $14\cdot4=56$ bytes of parameter payload. Two splats take 112 bytes and three take 168. A full model adds SH coefficients, gradients, optimizer state, tile lists, and temporary images. Text JSON also contains characters and keys. Here we measure exactly the numerical payload of the chosen representation.

</details>

### A copy or a second visible detail?

When two equal layers of the same color coincide in all coordinates, why does the center darken before two separate beads appear?

<details><summary>Reading the profile</summary>

With identical shapes the factor $w$ at any given pixel is shared. The covered fraction $1-(1-ow)^2$ increases with $w$ throughout the interval from zero to one. Wherever the single splat had its maximum, the pair retains a maximum at the same position. It is now higher. Two spatially separate peaks require different positions, different shapes, or later fitting that breaks the coincidence. In a red-channel profile this extra blue coverage looks like a deeper valley.

</details>

### A crumb behind an opaque wall

A rear splat has peak opacity 0.9. At our pixel the foreground has $\alpha=1$. What could this pixel tell us about removing the rear splat? What if the foreground alpha falls to 0.2 in a different view?

<details><summary>Following the remaining transmittance</summary>

In the first case $T=1-1=0$. The rear contribution vanishes at any rear alpha. This pixel gives no evidence about whether that detail exists. In the other view $T=0.8$. If the pixel lands at the rear center, its weight is now $0.8\cdot0.9=0.72$. Removal could change that image substantially. A threshold based only on visibility in a single view might mistake an occluded detail for a redundant one.

</details>

### Two decisions with the same row count

After an automatic pass the counter displays two splats again. How could we distinguish “nothing happened” from “the scene was restructured” without seeing its history?

<details><summary>Reading the numbers in a row</summary>

The first scene's broad row had $x=-0.16$, $s_x=0.63$, $o=0.77$. The crumb had $o=0.015$. After the pass the centers are −0.5695 and 0.2495, both horizontal scales are 0.39375 and both opacities are 0.77. Frontal error is about 0.003488 instead of 0.004677. The parameter payload stays at 112 bytes. Comparing positions, widths and a rendered image exposes a structural change that the counter alone missed.

</details>

title: 18. Two ways to render the same frame

cells.source: Five colored splats sit on white. The upper-left corner is almost empty, yet the renderer from lesson 14 still evaluates all five splats at every pixel. A sideways camera move shifts the empty space as well. Which work can be skipped depends on the current view.

## What belongs in a cell

Cutting the image into squares gives us *tiles*. Pale cells on the list map are nearly empty. Darker blue cells intersect more splats. Cells along the border can be shorter or narrower. Changing the tile size changes the number of pairs to test while preserving the pixels. Tightening a splat’s cutoff changes the image itself.

display(tiles_figure(lang=lang))
plt.close()
controls(lambda tile, k, angle: tiles_figure(int(tile), k, angle, lang),
         tile=[8, 4, 16, 32], k=(1., 4., .1, 3.), angle=(-45, 45, 1, 0))

### One object in memory, several addresses on the screen

The previous lesson counted Gaussians. This lesson introduces a different counter which often reads much higher. There are only five objects in space, each with one 3D center. Projection turns its center and shape into a screen footprint. One footprint can cross several screen cells. Each cell gets a short entry saying which object reaches it. The object was never cloned and the scene acquired no extra material. A list describes the current frame. After the camera moves, an old entry may correspond to empty space.

The pixel renderer in lesson 14 starts with “how much red, green and blue reached this location?” A tiled renderer starts a step earlier. Which objects are worth asking about in this part of the picture? Even for a pixel far from the splat, the earlier program subtracted coordinates, measured distance in the stretched local axes, evaluated an exponential, multiplied by opacity and updated the color. All of that work can go toward a value that looks white once rounded for display.

There are two separate decisions here. First comes a distance beyond which a contribution may be set to zero. That changes the footprint we have asked to draw. Then, for an already chosen boundary, we can gather candidates in advance. That changes how the chosen frame is evaluated. A visual check that two pictures look similar can easily mix up these choices. We will have three reference images. One retains infinite tails, one tests all five splats with truncation, and one draws that same truncated model using lists. Each pairwise comparison answers a different question.

## Where a soft splat ends

Strictly speaking, it never does. On a bell centered at 9 with width 2, sample 13 is $(13-9)/2=2$ widths from the center. Squaring 2 gives 4. Dividing by −2 gives −2, and the exponential turns this into $e^{-2}\approx0.1353$. At three widths the weight is still positive, $e^{-9/2}\approx0.0111$. With opacity 0.8, alpha at that boundary is about $0.8\cdot0.0111\approx0.0089$.

An ellipse has two displacements. Suppose the projected center is $m=(9,6)$ and the horizontal and vertical widths are 2 and 1 pixels. At $p=(12,7)$ the offsets are 3 and 1 pixels. Squared distance in units of the splat’s own widths is

$$
q=(3/2)^2+(1/1)^2=2.25+1=3.25.
$$

With cutoff $k=2$, this passes the test $q\le k^2=4$. Its weight is $e^{-3.25/2}\approx0.197$. For a rotated ellipse, lesson 13 gives $q=(p-m)^T S^{-1}(p-m)$, with $S$ the screen covariance in squared pixels. Its inverse removes the units of scale. Both $q$ and $k$ are dimensionless. Both renderers set the weight to zero outside this boundary.

q = (3/2)**2 + (1/1)**2
print("q =", q, "weight =", np.exp(-q/2))
assert q < 2**2 and np.exp(-9/2) < .012

### A boundary, a box, and a few extra tests

The small example appears on a pixel grid below. Dots mark the integer centers that pass the exact test. Orange marks the two-width contour. The dashed box is used when preparing tile lists. Its upper left pixel is $(5,4)$. Relative to the center it is two widths left and two widths up. Squared distance is $(-2)^2+(-2)^2=8$. The box covers 9 columns and 5 rows, or 45 pixel centers, whereas only 25 pass the ellipse test. The other 20 are the price of an easy bounding calculation. A pixel can safely fail a later test. Rejecting a needed pixel early would lose its contribution for good.

The chosen boundary condition is $q\le4$, including equality. The extreme points $(5,6)$ and $(13,6)$ therefore still get nonzero weight. The first allowed integer coordinate comes from rounding the left edge **up**, and the last from rounding the right edge **down**. Moving the center 0.2 pixels right gives the horizontal interval $[5.2,13.2]$. Integer centers run from 6 through 13. The tile range must also intersect the actual screen. A negative column cannot become an image pixel.

A rotated long axis usually runs diagonally while tiles remain aligned with the screen. The box width therefore needs the variance along the screen horizontal. Suppose the native scales are 2 and 1 pixels and both axes turn by 45°. The horizontal projections of those scales have lengths $2/\sqrt2$ and $1/\sqrt2$. Adding squares gives $S_{xx}=4/2+1/2=2.5$. The two-width boundary reaches $2\sqrt{2.5}\approx3.16$ pixels to either side. Equal horizontal and vertical bounds at this angle give a square box around a **slanted, elongated** footprint. Evaluating the shape inside still takes the full matrix, including its cross term.

from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse, Rectangle
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:13, 0:17]
q_grid = ((xx-9)/2)**2+(yy-6)**2
inside = q_grid <= 4
box = (abs(xx-9)<=4) & (abs(yy-6)<=2)
assert np.all(~inside | box)
print("pixel centers: box =", int(box.sum()), "ellipse =", int(inside.sum()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4), constrained_layout=True)
ax.scatter(xx, yy, s=7, color=".83")
ax.scatter(xx[box & ~inside], yy[box & ~inside], marker="x", color="#8675a8")
ax.scatter(xx[inside], yy[inside], color="#38679a", s=20)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5,4), 8,4, fill=False, linestyle="--", color="#5c7182"))
ax.add_patch(Ellipse((9,6),8,4,fill=False,edgecolor="#d57236",lw=2))
for edge in (3.5,7.5,11.5,15.5): ax.axvline(edge,c=".72",lw=1)
for edge in (3.5,7.5,11.5): ax.axhline(edge,c=".72",lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="u (px)",ylabel="v (px)",aspect="equal",ylim=(12.5,-.5),
       title="Какие пиксели получат цвет?" if lang=="ru" else "Which pixels receive color?")
plt.show()

## From an ellipse to a tile list

At two widths the same splat reaches from $9-2\cdot2=5$ to $9+2\cdot2=13$ horizontally and from $6-2\cdot1=4$ to 8 vertically. That rectangle encloses the ellipse. A corner sample can lie in the rectangle and still fail $q\le4$.

With 4-pixel tiles, columns 0–3 belong to tile 0 and columns 4–7 to tile 1. Integer division by 4 gives the tile index. Our rectangle reaches tiles 1, 2, 3 horizontally and 1, 2 vertically. One Gaussian gets $3\cdot2=6$ references. Its shape and color are stored once. For a rotated covariance the bounding half-width is $k\sqrt{S_{xx}}$, the half-height $k\sqrt{S_{yy}}$. These diagonals are variances along the **screen** axes. The square root brings the units back to pixels.

The depth test drops centers behind the near plane. At the edge of the screen, center position alone cannot reject a splat. A center at column −1 with a radius of 3 pixels still reaches column 2. Pixel 0 can receive color while the center lies outside the left boundary. The tile test therefore intersects the footprint rectangle with the image.

Each pixel now needs just one list. The nearest center comes first, then the next center in depth order. A splat receives weight $T\alpha$, where $T$ is the fraction of the ray still available. At $T=0.6$ and $\alpha=0.25$, the color weight is $0.15$ and $0.6(1-0.25)=0.45$ passes through. The order affects the color, so all tiles preserve the same depth ordering.

sc = small_scene()
cam = orbit(0, 73, 57)
slow, brute = finite_render(sc, cam, 73, 57, 8, 3, tiled=False)
fast, bins = finite_render(sc, cam, 73, 57, 8, 3, tiled=True)
print("pairs:", brute["pairs"], "→", bins["pairs"])
print("max |fast − slow|:", np.max(np.abs(fast-slow)))
assert np.allclose(fast, slow, atol=1e-12, rtol=0)

### What would be in a sorted array?

Ordinary Python lists work for the small scene. A paper-and-pencil version makes the GPU pass easier to follow. Suppose a red object R at depth 5 m reaches tiles 0 and 1. Blue B at 2 m reaches only tile 1. Green G at 4 m reaches only tile 0. Projection yields **three** sets of parameters, whereas distributing the addresses yields **four** entries. The entry count is the sum of overlaps rather than the number of objects times the number of tiles.

| Before sorting · tile, depth, object | After sorting |
|---|---|
| 0, 5, R | 0, 4, G |
| 1, 5, R | 0, 5, R |
| 1, 2, B | 1, 2, B |
| 0, 4, G | 1, 5, R |

The key has two parts. Tile IDs are compared first. Within one tile we compare center depths, putting the nearest first. Tile zero takes array positions 0 and 1. Tile one takes 2 and 3. The ranges can be written $[0,2)$ and $[2,4)$. A square bracket includes the left endpoint and a round one excludes the right endpoint. Red appears twice under the same object ID. Its color is read from one parameter row even though two groups of pixels process it.

At a pixel in tile 1, suppose blue has local alpha 0.5 and red has alpha 0.6. The background is white. Blue receives a weight of 0.5, leaving $0.5\cdot0.6=0.3$ for red. The background takes $0.5\cdot0.4=0.2$. Red intensity is $0.3+0.2=0.5$, green $0.2$, and blue $0.5+0.2=0.7$. A list built by merely appending red first and never sorting would make the image redder. Sorting matters for correctness even if every bound is perfect. The depth in the key belongs to the center. A common ordering for the entire tile is an approximation for extended, intersecting objects.

## Counting work and measuring time

With 73 × 57 pixels and five visible splats, the full loop considers 20,805 pixel–splat pairs. A cutoff makes some weights zero, but the distance test has already been paid for. At tile size 8 the lists leave 8,688 pairs to check. One extra candidate in a 64-pixel tile costs 64 tests. Smaller tiles save tests while larger tiles save list entries and setup. Python overhead and array sizes also affect elapsed time. The measurement first renders a warm-up frame, then takes the median of repeated wall-clock timings on this machine.

sides = [4, 8, 16, 32]
counts = [finite_render(sc, cam, 73, 57, side)[1]["pairs"] for side in sides]
plt.bar([str(s) for s in sides], counts, color="#4b78b8")
plt.axhline(brute["pairs"], color="#b86d37", linestyle="--")
plt.ylabel("pairs"); plt.xlabel("tile (px)"); plt.show()
print("CPU ms:", round(benchmark(lambda: finite_render(sc, cam, 73, 57)), 2))

## How 141 entries turn into 8,688 tests

There is a thin blue strip along the bottom of the list map. Eight does not divide the image dimensions evenly. Nine full tiles fit across, with a one-pixel-wide column left over. Seven fit vertically, followed by a one-pixel-high row. The map has eight rows and ten columns. The interior tile at indices $(3,4)$ contains four splat IDs. Each of its 64 pixels considers four candidates, which costs $64\cdot4=256$ distance tests. On the lower edge, tile $(7,4)$ has eight pixels and one splat. It adds eight tests. The lower-right tile has an empty list. Even its single pixel has no distances to compute.

This gives us a way to count work for any rectangular image. For each tile we multiply **its actual pixel area** by the length of its list, then add up the results. Multiplying all 141 entries by 64 gives 9,024. Those extra 336 tests belong to imaginary pixels beyond the right and bottom boundaries. The first count in the table below is the storage cost in entries. The second measures how often we have to check a distance. Going from 4 to 32 pixels cuts entries by a factor of about 26 while nearly doubling the number of tests. A small tile puts each splat into many lists. With a large tile, even a corner far from the splat gets its ID.

Now tile size stays at 8, and only the splat boundary changes. Each pixel in the error maps gets a color of its own. Of the three RGB differences we take the largest absolute value. Both maps use the same color scale so the cutoffs at one and three widths can be compared. The white background counts too. Dropping a weak blue contribution at the edge reveals more white, even where there are no other splats.

A radius of one width costs 1,728 tests, but the worst channel misses by roughly 0.628 on a scale of one. At three widths we get 8,688 tests and an error of around 0.0125. At four widths tests rise to 12,457 and the largest error falls to 0.00039. That is less than a step of 8-bit color, $1/255\approx0.00392$, in this frame. The number belongs to these five splats, their opacities and this view. A change of scene calls for a fresh comparison against the full Gaussian.

labels = {"ru": ("Полные хвосты", "Ошибка при k = 1", "Ошибка при k = 3", "плитка | записи | проверки | CPU, мс"),
          "en": ("Full tails", "Error at k = 1", "Error at k = 3", "tile | entries | tests | CPU ms")}[lang]
print(labels[3])
for side in [4, 8, 16, 32]:
    _, stats = finite_render(sc, cam, 73, 57, side, 3)
    areas = np.array([[min(side, 57-y)*min(side, 73-x)
                       for x in range(0, 73, side)] for y in range(0, 57, side)])
    assert np.sum(stats["tiles"] * areas) == stats["pairs"]
    ms = benchmark(lambda: finite_render(sc, cam, 73, 57, side, 3), repeats=3)
    print(f"{side:4} | {stats['references']:7} | {stats['pairs']:5} | {ms:7.2f}")
full = render_scene(sc, cam, 73, 57)
errors = {}
for k in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    cut, stats = finite_render(sc, cam, 73, 57, tile=8, cutoff=k)
    errors[k] = np.max(np.abs(cut-full), axis=2)
    print(f"k={k}, tests={stats['pairs']}, max |ΔRGB|={errors[k].max():.6f}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3), layout="constrained")
axes[0].imshow(full)
for ax, k in zip(axes[1:], [1, 3]):
    im = ax.imshow(errors[k], cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=errors[1].max())
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1:].tolist(), shrink=.76, label="max |ΔRGB|")
for ax, title in zip(axes, labels[:3]):
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()

## Where the original paper fits

Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, and Drettakis combine three mechanisms. Trainable 3D Gaussians hold shape and appearance. Density control adds or removes elements. The rasterizer turns the current model into an image quickly. The image loss from earlier lessons sends gradients back through rendering into the parameters. Our teaching implementation exposes the list traversal directly.

The authors’ implementation first culls centers, projects the covariance and computes a screen radius. Each splat–tile pair produces a record carrying a tile ID and depth. After sorting, neighboring records for a tile form one range. A GPU thread block processes a patch of the screen, loading candidate splats into shared memory in batches. Threads shade their pixels in parallel. The reference also includes screen filtering, a small-alpha threshold, an alpha cap and early termination when little transmittance remains. Equality between our arrays tests the two **teaching** paths with one common cutoff. The milliseconds above measure this CPU and this image size.

[Paper and results](https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/) · [Tile preparation and sorting](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/diff-gaussian-rasterization/blob/main/cuda_rasterizer/rasterizer_impl.cu) · [Pixel processing on the GPU](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/diff-gaussian-rasterization/blob/main/cuda_rasterizer/forward.cu)

## What can be shared, and what the backward pass needs

With 256 pixels in a tile, many pixels need the same centers, colors and shapes. In the original GPU rasterizer a block of $16\times16$ threads loads a batch of candidates into the block’s shared memory. Each thread reads these parameters for its own pixel and keeps two numbers for a single channel, the accumulated color and the remaining transmittance $T$. At $T=0.02$, everything farther away can account for at most two hundredths of the total weight. Even replacing a black remainder with white could move the channel by at most 0.02. This is the basis for stopping when a pixel is nearly covered. Once every pixel in the tile has finished, further batches can be skipped altogether.

The backward pass has a different job. Did the front or back splat darken the frame? Take a single gray channel. The near splat has color 0.2, the far one 0.8, and the background is white at 1. Their opacities at this pixel are 0.5 and 0.6. Behind the front splat we see a mixture of $0.6\cdot0.8+0.4\cdot1=0.88$. The final gray is $0.5\cdot0.2+0.5\cdot0.88=0.54$. Adding one hundredth of opacity to the front splat replaces one hundredth of the mixture at 0.88 with its own color of 0.2. The channel changes by $0.01(0.2-0.88)=-0.0068$. Adding the same opacity to the far splat replaces white with 0.8, and only half the change makes it through the front layer. That gives $0.5\cdot0.01(0.8-1)=-0.001$. Even at one pixel the two parameters receive different signals.

In the original backward pass the tile traverses the same list from the far end. Each pixel’s saved transmittance and last contributor help recover the weights needed for derivatives. This avoids storing a separate image for every splat. Screen-space gradients then travel back through projection to scene parameters, as in lesson 16. Tiles help this traversal too. On a frame containing a few enormous overlapping transparent splats, the advantage can disappear. Every tile gets the same IDs, and enough light gets through for distant layers to matter.

## An experiment

What changes when tile size goes from 4 to 32 at the same cutoff? What if tile size stays at 4 but the splat stops at one width?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

The first change alters the lists and test counts. Pixel weights and colors stay equal. The second removes samples whose weights were still around 0.6. Wider gaps show through. The difference from the full bell comes from its new support.

</details>

## Three more small scenes

### One faint tail and ten faint tails

Ten identical black splats over white each give $\alpha=0.01$ at one pixel. How far from white is that pixel when the tails are kept?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

The first splat transmits 0.99 of the white, the second leaves $0.99^2=0.9801$. After ten, $0.99^{10}\approx0.9044$ remains. The splats themselves are black and add nothing to the channel. Dropping all ten gives 1 instead of 0.9044. The error of 0.0956 is much larger than the hundredth due to any one layer. A threshold on individual contributions does not guarantee the same bound for a full frame.

</details>

### A two-pixel border

A 10 × 4 frame is split into 4 × 4 tiles. From left to right, the lists contain two, three and one ID. How many entries are stored, how many pairs get tested, and what would the full loop cost if five splats were visible?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

The lengths sum to $2+3+1=6$ entries. The first two tiles contain 16 pixels each. The last has just $2\cdot4=8$. That gives $16\cdot2+16\cdot3+8\cdot1=88$ tests. Testing every pair would take $10\cdot4\cdot5=200$. Storing six entries saved 112 tests. Milliseconds also depend on how much time goes into constructing and traversing the lists.

</details>

### Five enormous panes

The same five splats grow to cover a 73 × 57 frame and intersect every tile. Center opacity is 0.1. Can the same savings be expected at tile size 8?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

All 80 tiles now hold five IDs. That takes 400 entries and puts the test count back at $73\cdot57\cdot5=20\,805$. The bounding rectangles discarded nobody. Even if every pane reaches peak opacity here, after five layers $0.9^5\approx0.5905$ of the light gets through, far from full coverage. Early termination has little to gain here. For a new scene it makes sense to time preparation and rendering separately before choosing a tile size.

</details>

title: 19. Photographs, rays and COLMAP cameras

cells.source: Two photographs of a sculpture look almost identical. In one, a stone edge hides a patch of background. In the other, a sliver opens between them. Small shifts like this reveal depth. A blank patch of wall contributes little until we can identify the same location in another frame.

## Two cameras at a table

A tabletop setup isolates the geometry. The optical axes are parallel and the second camera sits 40 cm to the right of the first. Their separation B is the baseline. The orange ray passes through the mark in the right image and the blue through the mark in the left. Both rays lie in one horizontal plane. A small pixel error shifts their intersection. In the top view, depth increases away from the cameras.

display(rays_figure(lang=lang)); plt.close()
controls(lambda B, du, Z: rays_figure(B, du, Z, lang),
         B=(0,1,.01,.4), du=(-4,4,.1,0), Z=(1,8,.1,4))

## What changes when the camera goes around the subject?

There are two plausible explanations for a single photograph. In the first, a red mark is two metres in front of the lens. In the second it is six metres away. Both lie on the optical axis and land in column 40. If the farther mark is three times as wide in the world, even its outline can match the nearer one. A perfectly sharp contour in a single photograph still leaves depth open.

The camera now moves 40 cm to the right without turning. Relative to the camera, the mark moves 40 cm to the left. The near mark shifts by $80\cdot(-0.4)/2=-16$ pixels. For the far one the shift is $80\cdot(-0.4)/6\approx-5.33$. The first images agreed; the two predictions for the second are over ten pixels apart. This shift is parallax. It supplies a second measurement that depends on depth.

Turning the lens in place also changes the pixel address. But the line in the world from the camera center to the mark stays put. Any point farther along it is still consistent with both views. Images can look very different and yet give weak geometry. What matters during capture is the path of the camera **center**. The perspective calculation also needs the orientation of its axes.

<details><summary>Which second exposure distinguishes the two distances?</summary>

With a 0.1 m baseline the predicted positions differ by $80\cdot0.1(1/2-1/6)\approx2.67$ pixels. With 0.4 m they differ by about 10.67 pixels. A one-pixel marking error consumes a much larger fraction of the first separation. The longer baseline helps while the same detail remains visible and recognizable in both views.

</details>

## Eight pixels become four meters

Let $X$ be the target’s rightward offset from the left camera in meters, and $Z$ its forward distance in meters. Focal length $f$ is measured in pixels. The principal point has horizontal coordinate $c_x$. In the right camera the same target is at $X-B$. The recorded image columns are $u_L,u_R$.

$$
u_L=c_x+fX/Z,\qquad u_R=c_x+f(X-B)/Z.
$$

Subtracting the right column from the left cancels the shared $c_x$. The numerator contains $X-(X-B)=B$. The column difference $d=u_L-u_R$ is called disparity. This gives $d=fB/Z$. Multiplying by $Z$ and dividing by $d$ isolates depth, $Z=fB/d$.

Here $f=80$ pixels, $B=0.4$ m, $X=0$, $c_x=40$, and $Z=4$ m. The left column is 40 and the right is $40+80(0-0.4)/4=32$. Their difference is $40-32=8$ pixels. Depth is $80\cdot0.4/8=4$ m. The pixel units cancel. Moving the right mark one pixel to the right makes $d=7$ and puts the target at $32/7\approx4.57$ m. At $B=0$ both rays start at the same point, so one mark cannot determine depth. With nonzero baseline and $d=0$, there is no finite intersection in this setup.

Cameras on a walk around an object also rotate. Each image mark then defines a ray from its own camera center in a direction determined by that camera’s parameters. Noise can make two rays miss one another. Reconstruction looks for a 3D point whose **projections** lie near the recorded marks across several images.

for B, shift in [(.4,0), (.4,1), (.05,0), (.05,1)]:
    uL, uR = 40, 40-80*B/4+shift
    print(B, shift, "→", triangulate(80,B,uL,uR))
assert triangulate(80,.4,40,32) == 4

## How much depth fits inside a pixel?

It is tempting to read 4.57 m as a new distance to the object. Yet the mark on the table did not move. Only the observation changed. A better question starts with the measured disparity of eight pixels. Which depths would agree if that difference could be off by one pixel? At the near end $d=9$ gives $Z=32/9\approx3.56$ m. At the far end $d=7$ gives $Z=32/7\approx4.57$ m. The interval is asymmetric about 4 m because the uncertain measurement sits in the denominator.

At a depth of 8 m, the same baseline produces a disparity of only four pixels. Disparities from three to five now imply depths from $32/5=6.4$ to $32/3\approx10.67$ m. The lens and the accuracy of the pencil mark have stayed the same. The subject's distance changed what we can infer. If each individual observation can be off by one pixel, two errors in opposite directions can change their **difference** by two pixels.

<details><summary>The disparity is two pixels and its error could also be two. Where is the far end?</summary>

The near end has a disparity of four and a depth of 8 m. At the other end the disparity approaches zero from above. The quotient has no finite upper bound. A distance of 16 m corresponds to the middle of the measured pixel interval. It conveys very little about the uncertainty in metres.

</details>

for d in (8, 4, 2):
    near, far = 32/(d+1), 32/(d-1)
    print(f"d = {d} px:  Z = {32/d:.2f} m,  [{near:.2f}, {far:.2f}] m")
disparities = np.linspace(1.5, 12, 150)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.3, 3.1), layout="constrained")
ax.fill_between(disparities,32/(disparities+1),32/(disparities-1),alpha=.25)
ax.plot(disparities,32/disparities)
ax.scatter([4,8],[8,4],color="#b36639")
ax.set(xlabel="d, px",ylabel="Z, m",ylim=(0,25))
ax.grid(alpha=.2)
plt.show()

## What goes into a capture

Small camera steps keep recognizable fine details in neighboring photographs. A static matte object, diffuse light and sharp exposures make corresponding points easier to recognize. A second arc at another height opens up the top surface. Rotating the camera in place changes its direction while barely moving its center. The rays then constrain depth poorly. Very large steps lose shared details. Glass, a pedestrian, a repeated ornament or a highlight can produce convincing matches that belong to different world points.

Motion blur erases distinctive corners. Automatic exposure can turn the same wall from dark to light between frames. A small reprojection error on visible points says little about an unseen back surface. Before training we can already inspect both the images and the camera locations.

frames, seeds = photo_capture()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(8,2.8),layout="constrained")
for ax, index in zip(axes,[0,4,8]):
    f=frames[index]
    ax.imshow(f["rgb"]); ax.set_title(f["name"]+" · "+f["split"]); ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
print("train:", sum(f["split"]=="train" for f in frames), "test:", sum(f["split"]=="test" for f in frames))

## Inside a sparse reconstruction

Nine small real photographs of **struktur28_auto** from PhysicalAI-NuRec-PPISP (NVIDIA Corporation, CC BY 4.0) are included with the course. Their intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters are known. The cloud contains points. A point can have a track listing the images and 2D observation indices where it was recognized. The middle image view-04 is reserved for image evaluation. Camera poses are provided for the complete set, so this experiment measures image synthesis at a **known pose**. The [photograph notes](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/tree/main/data/photographic-example) document the source, license and transformations.

In a COLMAP text export, **cameras.txt** identifies the lens model. PINHOLE stores width, height and $f_x,f_y,c_x,c_y$. In **images.txt**, the first row of each image gives quaternion $(w,x,y,z)$, translation $t$, camera ID and filename. The next row stores triples of pixel x, pixel y and 3D point ID. ID −1 marks an observation with no reconstructed point. **points3D.txt** associates point IDs with position, RGB, error and track. ID 93 need not be row number 93.

COLMAP stores the **world-to-camera** transform $p_c=R p_w+t$. The camera center has zero coordinates in its own frame. Substitution gives $0=R C+t$. Moving $t$ across and undoing the rotation yields $C=-R^T t$. With an identity rotation and $t=(-0.4,0,0)$, the camera stands at $(+0.4,0,0)$. This often accounts for a sign error. Our renderer stores $C$ and the **camera-to-world** rotation $R^T$.

COLMAP’s first pixel center is $(0.5,0.5)$, while the first array sample here is $(0,0)$. Resizing width 160 to 40 uses $s=40/160=0.25$. The new focal length is $f'_x=s f_x$ and the principal point becomes $c'_x=s c_x-0.5$. Starting from $c_x=80$ gives 19.5, halfway between 19 and 20. Vertical coordinates use the actual ratio of heights after rounding. Shrinking only the image without updating $f_x$ would move its predicted pixels.

cam = frames[0]["camera"]
R = np.array(cam["rotation"]).T  # world to camera
C = np.array(cam["center"])
t = -R @ C
assert np.allclose(-R.T @ t, C)
print("C:", C.round(3), "f:", np.round(cam["focal"],3), "c:", cam["principal"])

# A measured feature and its projection in the original (160 x 120) training view.
from reconstruction_demos import ROOT
from geometry3d import project_point, quaternion_matrix
model_dir = ROOT / "data/photographic-example/sparse/0"
rows = [line for line in (model_dir/"images.txt").read_text().splitlines() if not line.startswith("#")]
header = rows[0].split()
observation = rows[1].split()
u, v, point_id = float(observation[0]), float(observation[1]), observation[2]
point_rows = (model_dir/"points3D.txt").read_text().splitlines()
point = next(line.split() for line in point_rows if line and line.split()[0] == point_id)
X = np.array(point[1:4],float)
world_to_cam = quaternion_matrix([float(v) for v in header[1:5]])
t0 = np.array(header[5:8],float)
intrinsics = next(line.split() for line in (model_dir/"cameras.txt").read_text().splitlines()
                  if line and not line.startswith("#"))
fx, fy, cx, cy = map(float,intrinsics[4:])
observed = np.array([u-.5,v-.5])
camera_point = world_to_cam @ X + t0
pred = project_point(camera_point,[fx,fy],[cx-.5,cy-.5])
wrong = project_point(camera_point+[.08,0,0],[fx,fy],[cx-.5,cy-.5])
print("point ID", point_id, "observed:", observed.round(3), "projected:", pred.round(3))
print("reprojection error (px):",round(np.linalg.norm(pred-observed),3),
      "after translation:",round(np.linalg.norm(wrong-observed),3))

The preceding calculation uses a real observed feature in the first photograph. Its ID connects two measured image coordinates to a 3D point. A world-to-camera transform and projection predict a pixel. Adding 0.08 scene units to the camera transform’s horizontal translation deliberately moves this prediction away from the observation. The final line reports both error lengths in pixels.

## Following one feature through three files

Some edges on the sculpture meet in dark corners that are easy to recognize. A detector picks out a local feature and describes the appearance around it numerically. Matching looks for similar descriptions. Two windows on the same building may look almost identical, so a descriptor match is only a candidate. If most matches agree with one relative camera pose and a pair lands somewhere completely different, geometric verification can reject that pair. Even the survivors are worth examining on the photographs.

An image takes up two lines in `images.txt`. The first identifies its file, camera and pose. The second repeats triples of horizontal coordinate, vertical coordinate and point ID. In a standard export, a negative ID denotes an observation without a reconstructed 3D point. In the other direction, `points3D.txt` identifies the images and observation indices in which each point was seen. An ID can be 148 even if there are only 117 points. Filtering leaves gaps. Reading the 148th row would be a mistake.

Point 148 has four observations in this capture. Two locate a point in space. A third lets us see where it lands. The experiment below uses images 80 pixels wide. In the original file for a 160-pixel image, coordinates are measured from the left edge. For example, $u=100.08$ becomes $100.08\cdot80/160-0.5=49.54$ in array coordinates. Subtracting half a pixel moves the origin from the pixel edge to its center. The way back to full-resolution file coordinates adds the half first and then divides by the scale. Reversing those operations changes the answer.

In the enlarged patches the orange cross is an observation; the blue ring is the projection of the reconstructed point. Moving the second cross horizontally changes the reconstruction. The cross in image 07 stays put. That image is reserved **for checking this pair of rays**. It did take part in estimating the full sparse model. The photograph `view-04` remains reserved for a different experiment, evaluating the trained scene.

views80, _ = photo_capture(max_side=80)
track = inspect_photo.feature_track()
display(inspect_photo.track_figure(views80,track,lang=lang)); plt.close()
controls(lambda partner, offset: inspect_photo.track_figure(views80,track,partner,offset,lang),
         partner=[8,6], offset=(-3,3,.1,0))

## From a mark to a ray and back to a mark

The first image provides $(u,v)$. Subtracting $(c_x,c_y)$ measures the offset from the optical axis. Dividing the horizontal difference by $f_x$ and the vertical one by $f_y$ gives the offsets **one camera unit forward**. Together with that forward unit they form a direction, $((u-c_x)/f_x,(v-c_y)/f_y,1)$. Its length is arbitrary. At depth two all three numbers could double and still give the same pixel. Multiplying by the camera orientation expresses the direction in the world. Dividing by its length leaves a unit arrow.

The first camera stands at $A$, the second at $B$, with unit arrows $r$ and $s$. Traveling a distance $a$ along the first ray reaches $A+ar$. The second gives $B+bs$, with its own travel distance $b$. Perfect observations would put both expressions at the same point. Moving the known terms across gives $ar-bs=B-A$. On the left, two known directions have unknown lengths. On the right is the known vector between the camera centers. Three coordinates yield three equations. Noise usually prevents two lengths from satisfying all three simultaneously.

The `lstsq` call chooses lengths that minimize the sum of the three squared discrepancies. The resulting points are the closest points on the two lines. Their midpoint supplies a hypothesis that we can project into image 07. This construction is simple enough to check by hand. When COLMAP refines a model, it minimizes errors **in the images** rather than distances between pairs of lines in the world.

For images 03 and 08 with zero offset, the third cross is near $(38.392,39.528)$ and the prediction is $(38.231,39.894)$. The distance is $\sqrt{(-0.161)^2+0.366^2}\approx0.40$ pixel. Shifting the second mark by three pixels increases it to about 2.01 pixels. With images 03 and 06 the same shift gives about 3.44. The real photographs are more complicated than parallel cameras at a table. Both camera orientations and the direction of the marking error matter.

<details><summary>Can a zero gap between two rays still produce the wrong point?</summary>

Yes. A wrong match in the right image might land farther along the same epipolar line, the set of possible projections of the left ray. The rays can literally intersect, just at a different depth. A third image from another position checks that false intersection. Agreement in local appearance across all three images lends further support.

</details>
