cells.source:
## A new set of photographs

For a static scene the detector first finds image features. Matching proposes pairs and geometric verification rejects inconsistent matches. The mapper registers cameras, triangulates points and refines camera and point parameters jointly against reprojection errors. An error here is the distance from the observed pixel to its predicted location. An offset of 3 pixels horizontally and 4 vertically has length √(9+16) = 5 pixels.

The commands below use an installed COLMAP. The raw photos are in capture/input; the empty capture/sparse and capture/text directories already exist. `exhaustive_matcher` considers all image pairs, which suits a small collection. If mapping produces several disconnected components, the example’s directory 0 stands for the connected model containing the relevant views.

```sh
colmap feature_extractor --database_path capture/database.db --image_path capture/input
colmap exhaustive_matcher --database_path capture/database.db
colmap mapper --database_path capture/database.db --image_path capture/input --output_path capture/sparse
colmap image_undistorter --image_path capture/input --input_path capture/sparse/0 --output_path capture/undistorted --output_type COLMAP
colmap model_converter --input_path capture/undistorted/sparse --output_path capture/text --output_type TXT
```

The course loader now reads `capture/text` and `capture/undistorted/images`. The undistorted model matters because our camera implements perspective division alone. A distorted photograph and an ideal pinhole camera disagree most near the edges. A large capture can be downsampled for a small experiment. The loader handles image resampling and camera scaling together.

[COLMAP commands](https://colmap.github.io/cli.html) · [Model format](https://colmap.github.io/format.html) · [Capture and reconstruction](https://colmap.github.io/tutorial.html)

## An experiment

Two reconstructions have the same mean reprojection error. In one the cameras barely move; in the other they follow an arc around the subject. Do they determine depth equally well?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

In the first capture, moving a point along the viewing ray hardly changes its image. A small image error can coexist with large depth uncertainty. The second capture intersects rays from different directions and constrains the position more tightly. Track lengths, camera layout and the photographs help explain the difference.

</details>

## What can be fixed before the first Gaussian appears?

The sparse model now exists. One meaningful count is how many **distinct views** observe a feature. Two observations give a pair of rays. A third adds an independent place where the point should land. But ten exposures taken almost in place still give a weak intersection. Track lengths make sense alongside camera positions and coverage of the subject. In this capture, 79 of the 117 points have exactly three observations. That describes the connections in the data. It cannot establish that the top of the sculpture or the space behind it has been recovered.

There is another freedom that is invisible in the photographs. Doubling the camera baselines and the world geometry doubles both horizontal offsets and depths. The ratio $X/Z$ stays the same. Measuring the statue in centimetres requires a known dimension, a measured baseline or some other external scale. That is why the baseline at the table is in metres while the gap in the photographic experiment is in reconstruction units.

<details><summary>Only 12 of 40 photographs registered, yet those twelve have a small error. What is worth examining before training?</summary>

The names and positions of the registered images come first. If they cover only the front arc, the small error describes the features visible from the front. Shared tracks at the end of that arc come next. A gap between the last sharp side view and a distant rear view can leave two disconnected models. A few overlapping photographs between arcs supply information that more training iterations cannot add. If matches do exist but consistent directional errors remain near every image edge, the lens model or an inconsistent resize is a better suspect.

</details>

Three things move on to the next lesson: the images, the cameras in a common coordinate system and the sparse colored points. An empty patch in the cloud only means that no reliable track was recovered there. Some gaps can still be filled during training if the cameras actually see the region.

title: 20. From photographs to a static scene

cells.source: Nine photographs of a sculpture are on the table. Their camera poses are known. One image can stay face down while the other eight guide the fit. Turning it over at the end shows what the model managed to learn about the space between cameras.

## The starting point

The colored-splat experiment starts with known centers and sizes. All splats are gray. Each color step sees three training views together. In the photographic capture, the centers come from sparse reconstruction. Changing the selected camera shows another image of the same model. A sideways camera shift opens a further view without a reference photograph. The browser fits RGB with geometry fixed. Later in the Python calculation, centers, three widths, rotation and opacity also become trainable.

## From one pixel to a first step

We can follow just the red channel. A splat starts at $c=0.5$. In this pixel its compositing weight is $w=T\alpha=0.6$. White background fills the remaining 0.4. The prediction is $P=0.6\cdot0.5+0.4\cdot1=0.7$. The photograph gives $Y=0.58$. The residual $P-Y=0.12$ has square $0.0144$. Adding 0.01 to the red channel would increase $P$ by $0.6\cdot0.01=0.006$. The current red is already too bright.

The derivative of squared error with respect to this color is $2(P-Y)w$. The 2 comes from the square, the residual retains its sign, and $w$ measures how much of the ray can see this splat. Numerically this is $2\cdot0.12\cdot0.6=0.144$. At learning rate 0.5, the new value is $0.5-0.5\cdot0.144=0.428$. Now $P=0.6568$ and the squared residual is about $0.00590$. The full calculation combines pixels from all training views. Empty areas carry little information about a particular splat.

Why are these first steps cheap? Fixed shapes give fixed weights. For pixel $j$ we store $w_{ji}$, its weight from visible splat $i$, and $b_j$, its fraction of white background. Then $P_j=b_j+\sum_i w_{ji}c_i$. The sum adds each splat’s contribution. With weights 0.6 and 0.1, background 0.3 and colors 0.5 and 0.2, the prediction is $0.3+0.6\cdot0.5+0.1\cdot0.2=0.62$. Each weight-matrix column corresponds to a splat and each row to a pixel. Summed products of these weights can be prepared just once, so another RGB update avoids reprojection. Each channel stays between 0 and 1.

w,c,b,target = .6,.5,.4,.58
pred = b+w*c
updated = c-.5*2*(pred-target)*w
print("color:", c, "→", updated)
print("loss:", (pred-target)**2, "→", (b+w*updated-target)**2)
assert (b+w*updated-target)**2 < (pred-target)**2

## Two different pairs of splats can make the same pixel

From the front, the first splat supplies a weight of 0.6 and the second supplies 0.1. White background accounts for 0.3. Suppose their red channels are 0.4 and 0.8. The pixel receives $0.6\cdot0.4+0.1\cdot0.8+0.3=0.62$. A different pair of colors, 0.45 and 0.5, gives exactly the same result. The first splat added $0.6\cdot0.05=0.03$ and the second took away $0.1\cdot0.3=0.03$. This camera has no evidence for choosing between the pairs.

From the side, the splats overlap differently. Their weights are now 0.2 and 0.5, with 0.3 still left for the background. The first pair predicts 0.78 and the second predicts 0.64. The side photograph measures 0.78. That is what the new camera brought to the fit: a measurement that **mixes the same two unknowns in different proportions**.

Starting with gray $(0.5,0.5)$, both cameras predict 0.65. The signed residuals are $+0.03$ and $-0.13$. Their mean square is $(0.03^2+0.13^2)/2=0.0089$. What if the first splat gets a little redder? The front pixel receives 0.6 times the increment and the side pixel receives 0.2 times the increment. The derivative of the mean square is $0.6\cdot0.03+0.2\cdot(-0.13)=-0.008$. The factor of two from the square cancels the division by two measurements. For the second splat the result is $0.1\cdot0.03+0.5\cdot(-0.13)=-0.062$. A small increase helps in both cases; the second splat receives a much stronger signal.

In the code, `W` holds two rows of weights. `W @ colors` assembles two pixels. `W.T @ residual` sends their errors back to the two splats. With fixed geometry, $W^\mathsf{T}(Wc-y)$ expands to $(W^\mathsf{T}W)c-W^\mathsf{T}y$. Here $y$ is the measured channel minus the background contribution. The two tables that contain no $c$ can be computed once. They appear as `gram` and `rhs` in `fit_colors`. Moving a center changes the weights, so the old table no longer describes the image.

<details><summary>What if the second picture is a copy of the first?</summary>

The two weight rows coincide. Repeating an exposure may average away measurement noise, but the two proposed color pairs still cannot be told apart. In the limiting case, a splat is hidden in every view. Its entire column of weights is zero, so changing its color leaves no trace in the pictures.

</details>

W = np.array([[.6,.1], [.2,.5]])
background = np.array([.3,.3])
red = np.array([.5,.5])
observed = np.array([.62,.78])
def two_view_loss(red):
    return np.mean((W @ red + background - observed)**2)
gradient = W.T @ (W @ red + background - observed)
eps = 1e-5
measured = [(two_view_loss(red+eps*d)-two_view_loss(red-eps*d))/(2*eps) for d in np.eye(2)]
print("∂L/∂c:", gradient, "  ΔL/Δc:", np.round(measured,6))
assert np.allclose(gradient, measured)
assert np.allclose(np.linalg.solve(W, observed-background), [.4,.8])

## A capture that travels with the model

Now the targets are real photographs from **PhysicalAI-NuRec-PPISP, struktur28_auto, NVIDIA Corporation, CC BY 4.0**. The course subset contains nine undistorted, adapted 160 × 120 images. Eight training photographs supplied 117 triangulated points at known camera poses. The ninth image’s pixels supplied neither those point locations nor their colors. For a quick fit we start from 24 points and reduce the images to 40 × 30. The initial splats are gray with equal opacity. A larger cloud can carry finer details at higher cost per step. [Photograph provenance and adaptations](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/tree/main/data/photographic-example)

Under the notebook's working directory, `static-scene-result/capture/` holds the PNGs, cameras, initial parameters and train/test labels. The neighboring file `static-scene-result/capture-browser.json` packs the capture for the website. After fitting, `static-scene-result/static-gaussians.json` contains the fitted parameters. The read-back check prints the model path relative to the working directory. In the notebook, `model_path.resolve()` returns the full local path including the filename.

For a separate capture, only the first line of the experiment below needs to change, where `photos, seed` are assigned. Suppose `IMG_0012.jpg` is the held-out photograph in that capture, processed with COLMAP as in lesson 19. With the `capture` folder in the working directory, the input becomes

```python
photos, seed = load_colmap(
    Path("capture/text"), Path("capture/undistorted/images"),
    max_side=40, max_points=24, test_names=["IMG_0012.jpg"],
)
```

The name must match its entry in `images.txt`, including its extension and any subdirectories. A held-out image amid near-identical burst shots tells little about a genuinely new view. The limits of 40 pixels and 24 splats keep the same image and model budgets as in the sculpture experiment.

When a personal reconstruction was estimated from all photographs, the loader split excludes held-out RGB from the gradients. Its initial 3D points and poses may still depend on held-out features. A stricter evaluation triangulates the initial cloud from training observations alone and supplies the test pose separately. The included example separates pixels and tracks that way, with original camera calibration supplied for the entire capture.

photos, seed = photo_capture(max_side=40, max_points=24)
out = Path.cwd() / "static-scene-result"
write_capture(out/"capture", photos, seed)
photos, seed = read_capture(out/"capture")
export_browser_capture(photos, seed, out/"capture-browser.json")
warm, color_loss = fit_colors(seed, photos, steps=12)
print("views:", len(photos), "splats:", len(seed["splats"]))
print("train RGB MSE:", round(color_loss[0],6), "→", round(color_loss[-1],6))

## Why color alone leaves a gray cloud unfinished

If a splat lands to the left of a stone edge, changing its hue cannot move it. The calculation now has a longer chain. Its 3D center moves into camera coordinates; dividing by depth gives the screen position. Shape and orientation determine the projected covariance. Each pixel gets a weight and transmittance, then RGB, a difference from the photograph and its square. PyTorch traces that chain backward. Every camera sees **the same** scene parameters. Each update first averages errors within a frame and then across the eight training frames.

The three widths must stay positive. We store unrestricted numbers $\ell$ and render the widths $s=\exp(\ell)$. At $\ell=0$, width is 1. At $\ell=-0.6931$, it is about 0.5 scene units. For opacity and color we store $a$ and render $1/(1+\exp(-a))$. At $a=0$ this gives $1/(1+1)=0.5$. Negative inputs move the output toward zero and positive inputs toward one. The four rotation coordinates are divided by their joint length as in lesson 12. Every update therefore yields a valid shape.

The single-color example used an ordinary gradient step. Across the different scene parameters below, Adam tracks an average direction and recent squared gradient magnitudes. Where one parameter repeatedly gives large gradients, normalization reduces its relative update. The code’s 0.017 sets the overall scale. This fit keeps 30 steps and a budget of 24 splats. Directional appearance, density changes and richer losses enter the larger implementation. The small experiment isolates the passage from sparse points to an adjustable image.

import torch
from reconstruction_fit import refine_scene
torch.set_num_threads(1)
trained, fit_loss = refine_scene(warm, photos, steps=30, rate=.017)
model_path = out/"static-gaussians.json"
model_path.write_text(json.dumps(trained, indent=2, allow_nan=False), encoding="utf8")
opened = json.loads(model_path.read_text(encoding="utf8"))
test_index = next(i for i,f in enumerate(photos) if f["split"]=="test")
f = photos[test_index]
h,w = f["rgb"].shape[:2]
assert np.allclose(render_scene(opened,f["camera"],w,h),render_scene(trained,f["camera"],w,h))
print("saved:", model_path.relative_to(Path.cwd()).as_posix(), " RGB MSE:", round(fit_loss[0],6), "→", round(fit_loss[-1],6))
display(view_figure(photos, opened, test_index, lang=lang)); plt.close()

## What changed in thirty steps?

The sculpture lets us keep three versions of **the same 24 splats**. In the first they are gray. The second has had 12 steps of color fitting. The third starts from the second and takes 30 more steps, this time changing color, geometry and opacity together. The three pictures below all use the held-out camera at 40 × 30. Switching viewpoints, splat budgets or resolution between columns would spoil the comparison.

Across the eight training images the mean squared error goes from about 0.3361 to 0.2542 after fitting color, then to 0.0564 after the joint fit. On the held-out view the corresponding values are 0.3501, 0.2652 and 0.0512. The improvement carried over at least as far as this camera. An angle absent from the capture contributes no evidence to the comparison.

Why does freeing the shapes make such a difference? A gray splat on white has a limit. At a pixel where its weight is 0.2, even a black splat produces $0.2\cdot0+0.8\cdot1=0.8$. No color update can reach a dark patch measuring 0.18. Moving the center, widening the footprint or raising opacity can increase the weight. They have different consequences for neighboring pixels: a shift moves an edge, widening spreads coverage on both sides, and higher opacity also conceals deeper layers. A single ray often cannot distinguish the causes.

stages = [seed, warm, opened]
labels = ["Старт", "Только RGB", "Все параметры"] if lang=="ru" else ["Initial", "RGB only", "All parameters"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(10,3),layout="constrained")
axes[0].imshow(f["rgb"]); axes[0].set_title(f["name"])
for ax, model, title in zip(axes[1:], stages, labels):
    pred = render_scene(model,f["camera"],w,h)
    ax.imshow(pred)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nMSE {np.mean((pred-f['rgb'])**2):.4f}")
    print(title, {split:round(np.mean([row["mse"] for row in evaluate(model,photos,split)]),5)
                  for split in ("train","test")})
for ax in axes: ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

## What the viewer opens

**static-gaussians.json** stores three center coordinates, three scales, four rotation coordinates, three color channels and one opacity per splat. Camera data stays with the capture because an image depends on both the scene and the observer. In the web lab, `capture-browser.json` goes into the local JSON field first, followed by `static-gaussians.json` in the same field. The browser uses the capture’s cameras to draw the imported model. A held-out photo can be compared with its render before shifting the camera. At a new pose the error readout disappears because there is no corresponding measurement. The browser accepts 2 to 32 frames, including at least one training and one held-out frame, up to 128 × 128 pixels per frame, and up to 128 splats. There is also a cap on the total computation size of a capture. A larger shoot can stay in Python while a selection of its cameras goes into the viewer. Both files stay on the device.

The website opens on the held-out photograph. Its dataset menu also offers **“Trained sculpture · 117 splats”**. This model ran for 1,200 steps on the same eight views, sampling 256 training pixels per step. It opens directly for inspection and export. At full evaluation resolution, 80 × 60, its MSE on view-04 is about 0.00982 or 20.08 dB. The browser compares this trained scene with the same 80 × 60 photograph. [Training the 117-splat model](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/blob/main/scripts/train_photo_reference.py)

Does the model resolve the stone’s details? Its splat budget is small, training directions are limited, and color is constant across viewpoints. Large masses and background color can emerge while narrow edges go missing. The next lesson measures that gap.

controls(lambda view, offset: view_figure(photos, opened, int(view), offset, lang),
         view=list(range(len(photos))), offset=(-.2,.2,.01,0))
print("model file:", model_path.name, " capture file: capture-browser.json")
cells.output: model file: static-gaussians.json  capture file: capture-browser.json

cells.source:
## Which splats painted this pixel of the sculpture?

This time the scene contains 117 splats. At column 40, row 30 of view-04 the photograph has RGB about $(0.180,0.180,0.161)$. To find where the render got its slightly different shade, we can follow the ray in depth order and record two quantities at each splat: how much visibility reached it ($T$) and which fraction of that remainder it covers ($\alpha$).

Splat 25 gives $T\alpha\approx1.0000\cdot0.4726=0.4726$. Only 0.4843 reaches splat 102. Its own pixel opacity is larger, 0.7529, but its share is smaller: $0.4843\cdot0.7529\approx0.3646$. The list below the photograph is sorted **by contribution**, after the depth traversal. The other splats and 0.0543 of white background complete the two leading weights. All weights together sum to one. Multiplying each by its RGB gives the final mixture $(0.164,0.167,0.151)$.

With geometry frozen, increasing just the red channel of splat 25 by 0.01 raises this pixel’s red by $0.4726\cdot0.01=0.004726$. The photograph was redder, so the change would help here. At the top left, splat 13 takes the lead and splat 25 carries only about 0.112 of the pixel. The same edit raises red there by just 0.00112. The decision to apply an update depends on all the training pixels. Here view-04 is a way to examine the already fitted model.

## The same photographs in the authors’ implementation

A full-size run uses the official project’s dedicated CUDA environment, rasterizer extension and a compatible NVIDIA GPU. The commands run inside the installed reference implementation and reuse **the undistortion results** from lesson 19. The files from `capture/undistorted/images` go in `scene/images`. The contents of `capture/undistorted/sparse`, including binary cameras.bin, images.bin and points3D.bin, go in `scene/sparse/0`. Image filenames continue to match the names in the model. The teaching loader reads the text export; the authors’ implementation uses the binary files.

```sh
python train.py -s scene -m models/sculpture --eval
python render.py -m models/sculpture
python metrics.py -m models/sculpture
SIBR_gaussianViewer_app -m models/sculpture
```

SIBR here is the installed viewer executable in the authors’ bin directory, with an .exe extension on Windows. The `-m` argument points at the **model directory** containing settings and the saved cloud in point_cloud/iteration_…/point_cloud.ply. Its PLY schema and parameterization differ from the teaching JSON. The official trainer changes density and learns spherical-harmonic appearance. With `--eval`, the ordinary COLMAP split holds out every eighth image in filename order. Our experiment explicitly reserves view-04. Comparing the two runs requires the same test poses, resolution and background. [Official project and dependencies](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting) · [Image split implementation](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting/blob/main/scene/dataset_readers.py)

## An experiment

After saving the scene, the camera moves. Which numbers in the Gaussian file must change?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

None. The renderer recomputes pixel positions, footprints and depth order. Training changes the stored scene; navigating a trained scene moves the observer.

</details>

## When a new capture turns into a white cloud

<details><summary>The loss barely moves. How can an empty projection be distinguished from a bad color?</summary>

One training camera is enough to overlay a handful of initial centers on its photograph and examine their depths. Negative depths for points in front of the camera suggest a pose conversion or axis error. Centers on the subject at the correct image resolution, yet nearly pure background in the middle of it, tell a different story. Temporarily doubling the width of one splat is a small diagnostic experiment. If its footprint appears on the expected detail, coverage or initial opacity deserves attention. If the footprint lands somewhere else, widening the entire cloud would mask the problem. The edit is reversible and it separates two explanations.

</details>

<details><summary>The training edges look sharp, but a patch detaches from the side. What makes the problem reproducible?</summary>

The named photographs with poses, fitting-view list, initial scene, fitted scene and the camera where the defect appears all matter. Replaying one short camera movement before and after the joint fit shows whether the patch was already present in the sparse cloud. Projecting a suspect point into several training photographs helps distinguish a bad initial track from a splat that drifted during fitting. If the scene looks convincing only in familiar views, an independent viewpoint supplies the next piece of evidence. Lesson 21 follows the score and the spatial pattern of that error.

</details>

title: 21. Held-out views, frame cost and visible artifacts

cells.source: Two models can look equally convincing from the front. After a small turn, one keeps a steady edge while the other reveals a dark spot in empty space. A single flattering frame hides the difference. We can inspect a static scene visually, with a difference map and with a measurement at a pose whose pixels did not participate in training.

## Where a detail went

Three views of the colored scene supply the gradients and two stay held out. Reference, rendered image and error brightness sit together. A slider amplifies one known change: wider splats, an extra opaque patch in front of the scene, or reduced green. These causes are deliberately controlled. In an actual reconstruction the same visual pattern is a clue for the next experiment.

## A fair image pair comes first

Held out means the frame’s RGB values were excluded from parameter fitting. The camera pose is known during evaluation. The three training views tell us how well the model fitted its inputs. The other two tell us how its shapes carry across viewpoints. Near-duplicates from a nearly stationary burst provide little evidence about a wide change of angle. Views used to choose learning rates or iteration counts belong to a separate validation set. Repeatedly tuning against a test frame changes its role.

The pixel comparison needs the same camera, resolution, crop and background. Suppose four normalized red target values are $[0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8]$ and the predictions are $[0.3,0.4,0.4,0.9]$. Subtracting the target at each position gives $[0.1,0,-0.2,0.1]$. Their sum is zero despite three wrong values. The absolute differences sum to $0.4$, so mean absolute error is $0.4/4=0.1$. The squares sum to $0.01+0+0.04+0.01=0.06$. Mean squared error is $0.06/4=0.015$.

Each RGB channel supplies one comparison. A 40 × 30 frame therefore contributes $40\cdot30\cdot3=3600$ numbers. A map pixel on the right shows the mean of three **absolute** errors. If only red differs by 0.3, its map value is $0.3/3=0.1$. Exposure, color space, background mask and crop can all affect the metric with identical geometry. These examples compare decoded RGB in [0,1] without a conversion to linear light.

reference = np.array([.2,.4,.6,.8])
predicted = np.array([.3,.4,.4,.9])
print("residual:", (predicted-reference).round(3))
print(scores(predicted,reference))
assert np.isclose(scores(predicted,reference)["mse"], .015)

## The same score can describe two different pictures

Two gray 16 × 16 squares start at 0.5 in all three channels. In the first copy, add 0.05 everywhere. In the second, add 0.2 inside a 4 × 4 patch. The pictures tell different stories: a small exposure shift across the frame, or a bright blemish on a gray surface.

In the first case each of the 256 pixels has squared error $0.05^2=0.0025$. In the second, just $4\cdot4=16$ of the 256 pixels changed. Each contributes $0.2^2=0.04$, so the frame mean is $(16/256)\cdot0.04=0.0025$. All channels agree, so averaging RGB changes nothing. The mean **absolute** errors do differ: 0.05 versus $(16/256)\cdot0.2=0.0125$. Squaring gave the occasional larger miss more influence. Either average still discards position. Moving the patch to a corner leaves both scores unchanged. The map shows whether the blemish landed on the silhouette or on empty background.

gray = np.full((16,16,3),.5)
shift = gray+.05
patch = gray.copy(); patch[6:10,6:10] += .2
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(7.4,2.55),layout="constrained")
labels = ["Эталон","Весь кадр","Один участок"] if lang=="ru" else ["Reference","Whole frame","One patch"]
for ax,im,title in zip(axes,[gray,shift,patch],labels):
    metric=scores(im,gray)
    ax.imshow(im,interpolation="nearest")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nMSE {metric['mse']:.4f}"); ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
assert np.isclose(scores(gray,shift)["mse"],scores(gray,patch)["mse"])

## Why decibels appear

PSNR uses the same MSE and reverses the direction of the scale. Let $A$ be the peak channel value in **the chosen representation**, for example 1. Then

$$
\mathrm{PSNR}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{A^2}{\mathrm{MSE}}\right).
$$

Squaring the peak puts it in the same units as the error. Dividing by the error in the example gives $1/0.015\approx66.67$. The base-10 logarithm asks which exponent of 10 gives 66.67. The answer is about 1.824. Multiplication by 10 gives 18.24 dB. Halving MSE adds $10\log_{10}2\approx3.01$ dB. An exact match has zero error and conventionally infinite PSNR. For bytes with peak 255, both $A$ and the measured MSE change. A numerator of 255 squared with a normalized denominator mixes the units.

A mean of frame-level logarithms differs from the logarithm of a mean error. For two equal-sized frames with MSE values 0.01 and 0.09, PSNR is 20 and about 10.46 dB. Their average is about 15.23 dB. Their pooled MSE is 0.05, giving about 13.01 dB. The table below keeps a separate row per camera so that a hard view remains visible.

## Another view of the same sculpture

The real photograph view-04 was absent from the eight training images. The larger example uses 117 splats initialized from sparse points and refined for 1,200 steps on sampled training pixels. Evaluation uses the full 80 × 60 image. Both images in each comparison must have the same dimensions. This model recovers more of the silhouette, although its edges and fine texture remain soft. When a capture stays on one side of an object, its back surface remains uncertain even in a large model. [Photographs by NVIDIA Corporation, PhysicalAI-NuRec-PPISP, CC BY 4.0](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/tree/main/data/photographic-example) · [Reproducible training](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/blob/main/scripts/train_photo_reference.py)

from reconstruction_demos import ROOT
photos, _ = photo_capture(max_side=80)
reference_path = ROOT / "site/dist/assets/reconstruction/photo-reference.json"
photo_model = json.loads(reference_path.read_text(encoding="utf8"))
image = next(f for f in photos if f["split"]=="test")
h,w = image["rgb"].shape[:2]
result = render_scene(photo_model,image["camera"],w,h)
print(image["name"], scores(result,image["rgb"]))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(8.6,3),layout="constrained")
for a,title,im in zip(ax, ["RGB", "117 × 3D","|Δ RGB|"], [image["rgb"],result,np.abs(result-image["rgb"]).mean(axis=2)]):
    a.imshow(im,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=1);a.set_title(title);a.axis("off")
plt.show()

## How much error falls on the subject?

The photograph has 80 × 60 pixels. A 40 × 30 box covers 1,200 of the 4,800 pixels, one quarter of the frame. It starts in the center, covering columns 20 through 59 and rows 15 through 44 inclusive. It is an ordinary rectangle containing both stone and some background. The same calculation works with an independently checked subject mask of any shape.

The map shows the root mean square deviation **at one pixel**. The three channel residuals are squared and averaged, then a square root restores the channel scale. For example, $(0.3,0,0)$ gives $\sqrt{(0.09+0+0)/3}\approx0.173$. Zero is dark and one is the top of the scale. A bright trace locates a discrepancy without telling which channel was too high.

With the box in the center, its MSE is about 0.011932. Outside it, MSE is 0.009113. The full-frame mean is $0.25\cdot0.011932+0.75\cdot0.009113\approx0.009817$. The factors 0.25 and 0.75 are area fractions. To find the share of **total** squared error inside, divide the first region’s contribution by the whole result. That gives $0.25\cdot0.011932/0.009817\approx0.304$, about 30.4%. A quarter of the frame accounts for just under a third of the error. Moving the box leaves global MSE unchanged. It changes the answer to a different question: where did the model lose image quality?

<details><summary>Can one carefully chosen rectangle settle which model is better?</summary>

A box chosen after seeing the predictions can easily favor one model on a convenient patch. A comparison can use the same predetermined mask, the same cameras and a shared map scale. Keeping the full frame beside the mask also reveals the cost of a local gain. A sharper piece of stone might come with a new blotch in the background.

</details>

## Reading different traces

**A floater.** An erroneous depth can hide in one image. Moving the camera slightly makes a dark patch slip off a surface and cover the background. A short arc around frozen geometry exposes the displacement. Excessive movement relative to the background points toward the patch’s depth; checking camera poses and feature tracks helps separate pose errors.

**Blur.** An enlarged Gaussian leaves residuals along an edge. Motion blur in the inputs, a coarse model or misaligned camera poses can leave a similar trace. Comparing the source sharpness and the projected sparse points helps distinguish them. Extra splats fitted to misregistered images can simply memorize the disagreement.

**Flicker.** A tiny change of angle suddenly changes color. Reordering translucent splats at similar depths, exaggerated directional appearance and insufficient filtering of small footprints can produce similar effects. A sequence of adjacent camera poses with the scene frozen exposes the jump. A single-frame score says little about it.

**Tint.** Reducing green leaves an error across a familiar surface. If the bias is similar in every view, exposure and RGB processing are worth isolating. If its sign changes with camera angle, directional color deserves a separate look.

The authors also report **SSIM** and **LPIPS**. SSIM compares brightness and the joint local pattern across windows. The gray windows $[0.2,0.8]$ and $[0.3,0.7]$ have the same mean, 0.5. Their deviations are $[-0.3,0.3]$ and $[-0.2,0.2]$. Mean squared deviations are 0.09 and 0.04, and their mean product is 0.06. In this window the brightness factor is 1; contrast and correspondence contribute $(2\cdot0.06+0.0009)/(0.09+0.04+0.0009)\approx0.924$. The small constant keeps the denominator away from zero. Full SSIM slides windows across the image and averages their scores. LPIPS measures differences between learned image features; its value depends on the network and preprocessing. All else equal, greater similarity gives higher SSIM and lower LPIPS. Comparisons with a published evaluation require the same metric implementations and protocol. [Authors’ evaluation code](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting/blob/main/metrics.py)

## A one-pixel shift or a blurred edge?

Consider a sharp step with brightness 0.2 on the left and 0.8 on the right. One “reconstruction” keeps the edge sharp but moves it one column to the right. The other keeps it in place and mixes in a quarter of each neighbor. In a small picture both can look like halos. The signed error $E=P-Y$ separates the cases. After the shift, one column shows 0.2 in place of 0.8, hence $E=-0.6$. Symmetric blur brightens the left edge from 0.2 to 0.35 and darkens the right edge from 0.8 to 0.65. It leaves two adjacent traces of opposite signs: $+0.15$ and $-0.15$.

On real stone the trace is a clue, not a diagnosis. A focal-length or resize error can move edges too, with a growing displacement towards the corners. Projecting the sparse points onto an original image separates some of these causes before training. If those projections drift towards the edges as well, the calibration, crop and resize deserve a look. If the points register and the photos are sharp, the shapes of the splats covering a small blurred region make a more informative next experiment.

Flicker calls for another measurement. Suppose a corresponding detail in two nearby photographs goes from 0.50 to 0.52, while the render goes from 0.48 to 0.68. The observed change is $0.52-0.50=0.02$. The predicted change is 0.20. The excess jump is $0.20-0.02=0.18$. Since camera motion usually displaces the detail, it has to be matched across the images. Comparing a fixed column number could compare stone in one frame with background in the other. On a path without photographs the jump is visible, but its deviation from a real change in highlight remains unknown.

edge = np.r_[np.full(6,.2),np.full(6,.8)]
offset = np.r_[edge[0],edge[:-1]]
blur = np.convolve(np.pad(edge,1,mode="edge"),[.25,.5,.25],mode="valid")
fig,axes = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(8,2.8),layout="constrained")
labels = ["Эталон","Сдвиг","Размытие"] if lang=="ru" else ["Reference","Shift","Blur"]
for a,title in zip((edge,offset,blur),labels):
    axes[0].step(range(len(a)),a,where="mid",label=title)
for a,title in zip((offset,blur),labels[1:]):
    axes[1].plot(a-edge,"o-",label=title)
axes[0].set(xlabel="u, px",ylabel="RGB"); axes[1].set(xlabel="u, px",ylabel="P − Y")
for ax in axes: ax.legend()
plt.show()
assert np.allclose((blur-edge)[5:7],[.15,-.15])

## What a frame costs

The teaching model stores 14 numbers per splat, $3+3+4+3+1$. Packed as four-byte float32 values, that is $14\cdot4=56$ bytes per splat and $117\cdot56=6552$ bytes for 117 splats. This is **the numerical payload**. The JSON file also stores keys, brackets and decimal digits. Python lists and dictionaries carry their own overhead in memory. Training additionally needs gradients, Adam state, intermediate images and the computation graph. Spherical harmonics change the parameter count in the full model.

The code below separately reports the actual JSON file size and times rendering without file I/O or plotting. A warm-up frame precedes the median of five timed calls. If a frame takes 20 milliseconds, one second contains 1,000 milliseconds, so $1000/20=50$ frames per second for sequential calls. A comparison of two renderers uses the same scene, cameras, resolution and hardware. A comparison of two candidate scenes can allow different splat counts. The renderer, hardware, trajectory and frame size stay fixed, and each scene’s count is recorded alongside its quality and timing. CUDA timings need synchronization or GPU events, or the clock can measure only the time taken to enqueue work.


A separate measurement enables tracemalloc around one warmed-up render. The peak counts the maximum simultaneously allocated bytes visible to Python’s allocation tracer, including library allocations registered with it. Timing runs separately. The already-loaded model, complete process memory, driver allocations and VRAM are outside this measurement.

ms = benchmark(lambda: render_scene(photo_model,image["camera"],w,h),repeats=5)
print("resolution:", w,h," · CPU median ms:",round(ms,3))
print("frames/s:", round(1000/ms,2))
print("float32 payload B:", len(photo_model["splats"])*14*4, "JSON file B:", reference_path.stat().st_size)

import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
try:
    rendered = render_scene(photo_model,image["camera"],w,h)
    _, peak_bytes = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
finally:
    tracemalloc.stop()
print("traced CPU render peak (bytes):", peak_bytes)

cells.source:
## An experiment

A larger model raises PSNR only on training views and takes longer per frame. Which comparison would show what actually improved?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

Both models can be rendered from the same held-out cameras, with the reference, both predictions and error maps on a common scale. Lower training error can mean a better-known detail, a memorized highlight, or an extra splat behind a surface. The held-out pair shows whether that improvement travels with the camera. Frame time and model size are measured separately under equal conditions.

</details>

## Where the experiment ends

View-04 comes with a reference RGB image, a model, a pose, a resolution and a comparison protocol. On a free orbit there is just the model and a moving camera. The two checks answer different practical questions: how far the prediction missed an observed view, and what begins to behave strangely in motion.

<details><summary>Which of two models, A and B, can serve a 30-frame-per-second viewer?</summary>

Suppose A renders in 22 ms and B in 38 ms on the same device at the same resolution. The frame budget is $1000/30\approx33.3$ ms. A leaves about 11.3 ms for the rest of the frame, while B exceeds the budget by roughly 4.7 ms even if its PSNR is higher. The median describes a typical frame. Smooth motion also depends on the slow frames along the same camera path. If B resolves a valuable detail, the next fair pair would compare both models at a common budget with the same camera, resolution and mask, with timing and quality shown side by side. Lowering the resolution only for B would change two conditions at once.

</details>

For another capture the result can be kept in concrete form: training and held-out frame names, the scene, render settings, a table by camera, a photograph with its error map and a short path through the trouble spot. A suspicion such as “the smallest splats flicker” then becomes testable. The scene and cameras stay fixed, only the filter changes, and the comparison uses the same region and motion. That closes the path from a single Gaussian to evaluating a whole static scene.

title: 22. Which moved, the camera or the splat?

cells.source: An orange splat slides to the right between two exposures. It could be travelling across a table. The same shift appears if the table stays put and the camera moves left. A fixed blue mark and a second camera give the two explanations different fingerprints.

## Two shutters

Cameras A and B face straight ahead on a moving bar. B sits 0.8 m to the right of A. The orange splat and blue mark are 4 m deep. The time control sets the instant A fires. With zero delay, B fires at exactly the same instant. Turning on the screen adds an opaque strip halfway to the splat.
display(motion_lab(22, lang))

## What one exposure measures

At time zero the splat sits directly in front of A. In 0.8 seconds at 1 m/s it travels $1\cdot0.8=0.8$ m. Positive means right. With A stationary, the horizontal offset from the camera is 0.8 m. The depth is $Z=4$ m, giving a ray slope of $0.8/4=0.2$. The focal length $f=80$ pixels turns that slope into $80\cdot0.2=16$ pixels. The central column is $u_0=48$, so the splat lands at $48+16=64$.

In a second shot the splat stays put and A moves left by 0.8 m. Their positions still differ by $0-(-0.8)=0.8$ m. Both stories put orange at 64. The blue mark is fixed at $X=-1.2$ m. In the first story it lands at $48+80(-1.2)/4=24$. In the second it lands at $48+80(-1.2+0.8)/4=40$. There is now a visible way to tell the motions apart.

Here is the common calculation. At time $t$ in seconds, $X(t)$ is the horizontal position of the splat and $C(t)$ that of the camera, both in metres. For constant positive depth the lengths in the fraction cancel. The answer $u(t)$ is in pixels.

$$
u(t)=u_0+f\frac{X(t)-C(t)}{Z}.
$$

cells.output:
v = +1, camera = +0 m/s   orange = 64.0, blue = 24.0 px
v = +0, camera = -1 m/s   orange = 64.0, blue = 40.0 px
v = +1, camera = +1 m/s   orange = 48.0, blue = 8.0 px

cells.source:
fig = motion_figure(22, lang, time=.8, object_speed=0, camera_speed=-1)
plt.show()

## Where the wrong depth comes from

With a stationary bar, A sees orange at 64. At the same instant B sits at $C_B=0.8$ m, directly opposite the splat, so $u_B=48$. The difference $d=u_A-u_B=16$ pixels is called disparity. Subtracting two projections of the **same position** cancels the splat coordinate $X$. The horizontal camera separation $b=C_B-C_A$ remains. For positive $d$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
d&=\frac{f}{Z}\big((X-C_A)-(X-C_B)\big)=\frac{fb}{Z},\\
Z&=\frac{fb}{d}=\frac{80\cdot0.8}{16}=4\ \mathrm{m}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now B fires 0.2 seconds late. The splat has reached $X=1$ m. Camera B sees $48+80(1-0.8)/4=52$. Treating these as synchronized samples gives $64/(64-52)=5.33$ m. Both recorded pixel positions are correct, but their rays met the splat at different times. A delay of 0.8 s makes the disparity zero. Dividing by zero yields no finite depth.

## What the frames leave out

The screen is 2 m away and the splat is 4 m away. Halfway along a ray, the horizontal coordinate is the average of its endpoints. For A this is $(0+0.8)/2=0.4$ m, inside the opaque interval from 0.28 to 0.52 m. For B it is $(0.8+0.8)/2=0.8$ m, beyond the edge. The right frame still shows the center. In the left frame it is hidden. An orange tail peeking around an edge does not by itself give the hidden center's position.

fig = motion_figure(22, lang, gate=True)
plt.show()

**What is still unknown?** Two synchronized views recover the center at 0 and 2 s. Do those observations determine its position at one second?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

Each pair constrains depth at its own exposure time. The interval between exposures is empty. The splat could move steadily, slow down or swing sideways and still reach the second position on time. Drawing a straight line between the centers adds a motion assumption. The next splat makes the cost of that assumption visible in pixels.

</details>

title: 23. One Gaussian between three photographs

cells.source: The orange splat starts on the left and ends on the right. Joining its two centers with a straight line makes a perfectly smooth animation. A third exposure halfway through reveals the miss. The silhouette is changing too. Center motion and shape can be followed separately.

## Two marks already determine a line

The camera is the one from the previous experiment. The known depth is 4 m, the central column $u_0=48$ px and the focal length $f=80$ px. At 0 and 2 seconds the orange center appears at columns 38 and 62. In the first exposure the offset is $38-48=-10$ px. Dividing by 80 gives a slope of $-0.125$, and multiplying by 4 m gives a position of $-0.5$ m. For the second exposure, $(62-48)\cdot4/80=0.7$ m. The two images have yielded two spatial measurements.

The splat went from $-0.5$ to $0.7$ m in 2 s. The difference is $0.7-(-0.5)=1.2$ m, so the average velocity was $1.2/2=0.6$ m/s. At that constant velocity the center would reach $-0.5+0.6=0.1$ m after one second. The dashed line joins the observations. Green shows the reference motion withheld from the fit. A vertical mark in the image shows its projected center.
display(motion_lab(23, lang))

pixels = np.array([38., 62.])
positions = (pixels - motion.U0) * motion.DEPTH / motion.F
v = (positions[1] - positions[0]) / 2
print('x (m)', positions, '  v (m/s)', v, '  x(1) (m)', round(positions[0] + v, 3))

fig = motion_figure(23, lang)
plt.show()

## One more exposure bends the path

Halfway through the interval the camera actually sees column 46. The measured position is $(46-48)\cdot4/80=-0.1$ m. The straight line missed by $0.2$ m or $80\cdot0.2/4=4$ pixels. How could a curve correct that miss while leaving both measured endpoints in place?

The number of elapsed seconds is $h=t/(1\,\mathrm{s})$. The units cancel in this ratio. The product $g=h(2-h)$ vanishes at $h=0$ and $h=2$, but equals one at $h=1$. Multiplying it by the middle measurement's displacement from the line puts a correction exactly where it is needed. Here $l(t)$ denotes the line and $x_1$ the middle position measured in metres.

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(t)&=-0.5+0.6h\quad\text{(m)},\\
x_1-l(1\,\mathrm{s})&=-0.1-0.1=-0.2\quad\text{(m)},\\
x_{\mathrm{fit}}(t)&=l(t)+(x_1-l(1\,\mathrm{s}))\,h(2-h).
\end{aligned}
$$

At half a second the line gives $-0.5+0.3=-0.2$ m. The correction has weight $0.5(2-0.5)=0.75$. Together they give $-0.2-0.2\cdot0.75=-0.35$ m, or column 41. This intermediate exposure tests both models at a time neither used for fitting.

## What rotates inside the splat

The splat stays at $z=4$ m and $y=0$. Its long scale starts at 0.24 m and grows by 0.08 m per second. After one second $s_x=0.24+0.08=0.32$ m. The transverse scale holds at 0.11 m and the depth scale at 0.08 m. All three stay positive throughout the displayed interval from 0 to 3 s. The long axis turns by $30^\circ$ per second around the depth axis. The camera looks along that axis and screen y points down, so the turn appears clockwise.

The renderer from lesson 14 takes four rotation components. For an axis of $(0,0,1)$ the angle is halved. Half of $30^\circ$ is $15^\circ$. The first component is $\cos(15^\circ)\approx0.966$, the last is $\sin(15^\circ)\approx0.259$ and the other two are zero. Scale and orientation follow prescribed paths here. The measured columns are used to recover the center trajectory.

## Beyond the last exposure

Between the observations, up to 2 s, the curve interpolates. Past the last observation it extrapolates. The synthetic reference follows a line plus $a\,t(t-2\,\mathrm{s})$, where $a$ has units of m/s². At $a=0.2$ three exact observations determine this parabola completely. A real splat might stop after the last exposure even if a parabola passed through all three observations perfectly.

If the middle observation is shifted by $+0.1$ m, its error is multiplied by $h(2-h)$. At 0.5 s that gives $+0.075$ m. At 3 s it gives $0.1\cdot3\cdot(-1)=-0.3$ m. Moving the middle mark right sent the prediction left and tripled the error. The gap between the splat and the green mark in the next image shows the shift.

fig = motion_figure(23, lang, time=3, middle=True, noise=.1)
plt.show()

**A change of numbers.** The actual motion is linear, but the middle observation is shifted by $+0.1$ m. Which fit is closer at 3 s?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

The line through the two accurate endpoints continues the true path. The parabola passes through all three measurements and misses by 0.3 m to the left. At 20 pixels per metre that is 6 pixels. Extra observations help when their uncertainty is also accounted for. This fit has to pass through even the corrupted observation.

</details>

title: 24. How a splat keeps track of its neighbour

cells.source: Two identical splats sit on a rotating part. Fitting two fresh centers in the next frame can make a convincing image. Which new center belongs to which old splat? The image alone may have no opinion.

## One image, two histories

Both splats have the same color, shape and opacity. At first their centers sit 0.4 m left and right of the midpoint. In the next frame there are splats in exactly the same places. Perhaps they both stayed still. Perhaps they traded places between exposures. The splat that starts on the left carries the label A, the one on the right B. The letters stand for persistent array indices. They do not appear in the image.

The code renders both final frames with the same compositor used for the static scene. In one history A has travelled 0 m, in the other $0.4-(-0.4)=0.8$ m. Swapping two contributions with identical colors leaves the pixel difference at zero to numerical precision.

## What a neighbour can tell us

An elongated shape makes A's orientation visible. Between exposures its long axis makes a quarter turn. If B sits on the same rigid part, the edge between their centers turns with A. In this experiment A sits at the origin of the current frame. Blue marks the tip of the rigidly rotated edge, green the true B and orange our estimate from measurements. The bend control lets the neighbour move relative to the part.
display(motion_lab(24, lang))

## Rotating an edge, in numbers

In the previous frame A was at $(-0.4,-0.2)$ m and B at $(0.4,-0.2)$ m. The edge from A to B comes from subtracting their coordinates component by component. Horizontally, $0.4-(-0.4)=0.8$ m. Vertically, $-0.2-(-0.2)=0$. The edge is $(0.8,0)$. When A moves to $(0,0)$, translating the part leaves the edge length alone.

The angle of the turn is $\theta$. Positive y points down, as in an image. A $90^\circ$ turn sends a rightward arrow downward. At an arbitrary angle the unit rightward arrow becomes $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. Multiplying each component by the length of 0.8 m gives the expected tip $r$. With $\cos90^\circ=0$ and $\sin90^\circ=1$ it lands at $r=(0,0.8)$ m.

The orange measurement in the current frame put B at $q=(0.4,0.6)$ m. The difference is $q-r=(0.4,-0.2)$ m. Its Euclidean length is $\sqrt{0.4^2+(-0.2)^2}=\sqrt{0.20}\approx0.447$ m. Placing B right on the mark would leave that much tracking error for a truly rigid turn.

fig = motion_figure(24, lang, strength=4)
plt.show()

## Combining the mark and the rotation

One coordinate is enough to see how the fit works. The trial position $b$, the measurement $q$ and the rotation prediction $r$ are all in metres. The fit adds the squared distance to the mark and a weighted squared distance to the rigid prediction. The weight $\lambda$ is nonnegative and dimensionless. At $\lambda=4$ a displacement of a given size away from the rigid neighbour costs four times as much as the same displacement away from the mark. Both terms are in square metres.

$$
L(b)=(b-q)^2+\lambda(b-r)^2.
$$

The derivative of a square from lesson 7 is twice the residual. The derivatives add, and their sum vanishes at the bottom of the bowl. Dividing both sides by 2, collecting the terms in $b$ on the left and factoring gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
2(b-q)+2\lambda(b-r)&=0,\\
b+\lambda b&=q+\lambda r,\\
b&=\frac{q+\lambda r}{1+\lambda}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The denominator stays positive even at zero weight. Horizontally the fit gives $(0.4+4\cdot0)/5=0.08$ m. Vertically it gives $(0.6+4\cdot0.8)/5=0.76$ m. The displacement from the rigid prediction has fallen to $(0.08,-0.04)$ m, about 0.089 m in length. The formula is the exact minimizer for this small squared-error problem.

## From one pair to Dynamic 3D Gaussians

Luiten and colleagues reconstruct the first instant as a static scene from multiple cameras. At later instants the same Gaussians update their centers and rotations. In the paper's model their size, color and opacity persist. Rendered images are compared with camera images. This fitting process does not need supplied point tracks. [Project and results](https://dynamic3dgaussians.github.io/)

The authors select each Gaussian's 20 nearest neighbours using positions in the first frame. A pair that starts closer together gets more weight. Three penalties serve different purposes. One compares the edge between consecutive instants after accounting for A's rotation, much as our pair experiment does. Another compares the changes in the orientations of A and B **themselves** over one step. Two splats can keep their positions but turn their long axes by different amounts. The third compares the **length** of the current edge with its length in the first frame. Small increments of stretch are then detectable even as they accumulate over many frames. [Three neighbourhood constraints](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.09713v1)

Our experiment supplies A's rotation and a measured position for B. The original fits many centers and orientations together using the images and local constraints. Squaring a distance in our small example makes a solution by hand possible. The paper's local rigidity expression uses the length of a vector residual. The public training code also allows a small color change with a penalty. [Authors' implementation](https://github.com/JonathonLuiten/Dynamic3DGaussians/blob/main/train.py)

fig = motion_figure(24, lang, strength=4, noise=0, bend=40)
plt.show()

**At a hinge.** The measurement is exact but the part bends an extra $40^\circ$ relative to A's turn. What does a strong neighbour weight do?

<details><summary>Worked answer</summary>

With zero noise the measurement is the true B. At $\lambda=0$ orange coincides with green. Increasing the weight pulls it toward the blue endpoint, which assumes rigidity. At $\lambda=4$ the two predictions receive weights in the ratio four to one. The estimated point travels four fifths of the way from the correct mark toward the wrong rigid prediction. Even good first-frame neighbours may move differently on opposite sides of a hinge.

</details>

title: 25. Bending a ribbon of five Gaussians

cells.source: Five colored splats lie in a line. Keeping five Gaussians for every frame would leave a stack of almost identical ribbons. What if we kept a single ribbon and a map of how far it bends? The map could then give us a picture between frames, too.

## One ribbon before and after the bend

The blue splat on the left has a horizontal coordinate of −0.8 m. The orange one at the opposite end sits at 0.8 m. All five centers start at height zero and depth 4 m. These rest coordinates are called **canonical** coordinates. The camera looks forward, and the image’s vertical axis points down. Raising the ribbon therefore means *subtracting* a distance from its $y$ coordinate.

The first picture always shows the rest ribbon. In the second, each splat gets its displacement from the same map. Changing the viewpoint turns both pictures together. The dot on the map stays put as long as the time and the selected splat stay the same.
display(demos.lab(25, "en"))

## Reading a value between four nodes

The map has two axes. Horizontal position runs along the ribbon, while time runs from bottom to top. To turn metres into a location inside a cell, we map the interval from −1 to 1 m onto the fraction from 0 to 1. Adding 1 m puts the left edge at zero. Dividing by the interval length of 2 m gives the orange center $u=(0.8+1)/2=0.9$. That is nine tenths of the way across. The recording lasts one second. At $t=0.5$ s the fraction of elapsed time is $v=t/(1\,\mathrm{s})=0.5$.

| Fraction of time | Left node, $u=0$ | Right node, $u=1$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| Start, 0 | 0 | 0 |
| End, 1 | 0 | 1 |

Each node stores a dimensionless number, called a *feature* here. We first move along the bottom row. The remaining distance to the right edge is $1-0.9=0.1$ of a cell. The left value gets a weight of 0.1 and the right one gets 0.9, giving $0.1\cdot0+0.9\cdot0=0$. On the top row the same weights give $0.1\cdot0+0.9\cdot1=0.9$. Halfway through the clip the rows contribute equally: $0.5\cdot0+0.5\cdot0.9=0.45$.

This is **bilinear interpolation**. The symbol $F$ stands for the sampled value. In $g_{ij}$ the first index is column $i$ and the second is row $j$, each either zero or one. The weights inside the brackets move across the ribbon. The weights outside move through time.

$$
F(u,v)=(1-v)\big[(1-u)g_{00}+u g_{10}\big]+v\big[(1-u)g_{01}+u g_{11}\big].
$$

At $u=0.9$ and $v=0.5$ the four weights are 0.05, 0.45, 0.05 and 0.45. They add up to one. If all four corners contain the same value, blending reproduces it exactly.

x = motion.ribbon()["splats"][-1]["center"][0]
u = (x + 1) / 2
print("u =", u, " F =", motion.field_value(u, .5))

fig = demos.field_figure(lang="en")
plt.show()

## Turning the number into a bend

A feature of 0.45 says nothing about metres yet. We give feature value 1 a lift of 0.8 m. The vertical offset becomes $\Delta y=-0.8\cdot0.45=-0.36$ m and the new center is $(0.8,-0.36,4)$ m. One unit of feature also means −35° of rotation, so the angle is $-35\cdot0.45=-15.75$°. For a rotation around the depth axis, the four entries from lesson 12 become $q=(\cos(\theta/2),0,0,\sin(\theta/2))$. Multiplying degrees by $\pi/180$ converts them to radians for sine and cosine. Half the angle is −7.875°, about −0.1374 radians. The first quaternion entry is roughly 0.991 and the last is about −0.137.

The long scale of the resting splat is 0.27 m. Suppose a unit feature increases it by 30%. The factor is $1+0.3\cdot0.45=1.135$, giving a new scale of $0.27\cdot1.135=0.30645$ m. Color and opacity stay fixed. Together these three rules are our **decoder**. They turn a map value into changes in center, rotation and scale. Every change starts from the same rest ribbon. Repeating the calculation with time paused leaves the splat in place.

## Where the model of Wu and colleagues goes further

Our map has an awkward property. Two splats with the same $x$ at different depths always receive the same bend. A query in the 4D-GS implementation has four coordinates $(x,y,z,t)$. They form six pairs: $xy$, $xz$, $yz$, $xt$, $yt$, $zt$. Each pair has a plane of learned values. Two points can fall together on the $xt$ plane yet separate on $zt$. The authors’ code interpolates the values and multiplies matching channels across planes at each resolution. If one channel reads $1,1,1,0.45,1,0.8$, the product is $0.36$. Results at different resolutions are joined into one list. [Interpolation in the authors’ implementation](https://github.com/hustvl/4DGaussians/blob/master/scene/hexplane.py)

A small neural network then predicts corrections to the canonical Gaussians. During training the rendered images are compared with observations. Four grid values and three hand-written rules make the journey of a single number visible here. The full method learns grid values, decoder parameters and the starting Gaussians from the frames. [Wu et al., 4D Gaussian Splatting, CVPR 2024](https://guanjunwu.github.io/4dgs/)

## Bending in the other direction

At 0.5 s, what changes if the upper-right node holds −1 instead of 1? Why does a different camera leave the answer for the center alone while changing the image?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

The top row gives −0.9 and the bottom one zero. Halfway through time the feature is −0.45. The vertical offset $-0.8\cdot(-0.45)=+0.36$ m points down. The long scale is $0.27(1-0.135)=0.23355$ m. Rotation changes sign to +15.75°. Only the rest center, the time and the nodes entered those calculations. The camera first appears in the next step, when the new ellipsoid is projected onto the screen.

</details>

fig = demos.field_figure(corner=-1, lang="en")
plt.show()

title: 26. Recovering motion from two stereo pairs

cells.source: The blue end of the ribbon barely moves. The orange end lifts and settles back down. Two fixed cameras saw the ribbon a quarter and three quarters of a second into the clip. There are no training frames in between. Where will the orange splat appear at 0.375 s, seen from the side?

## What the fit gets to see

The ribbon has the same five splats as before. Its rest shape, colors, initial positions and cameras are known. In the synthetic recording each center has a colored landmark. The fit receives the landmark IDs and their pixel coordinates. The generator keeps the actual 3D centers and a third camera’s images for evaluation. Finding matching landmarks in ordinary video would be a separate problem.

Camera and time move independently. The two alternatives are a static ribbon and a model fitted to the landmarks. Switching between them changes the picture on the right. The frame on the left still comes from the synthetic recording. Holding one control steady separates a change of viewpoint from a change of time before testing the two together.
display(demos.lab(26, "en"))

## Turning two pixels into one point

Both cameras have a focal length $f=64$ px and principal point $(32,24)$ px. The left camera is at the origin, the right camera displaced $B=0.8$ m to the right. Both look straight ahead. For the ribbon tip at 0.25 s, the horizontal pixel coordinates are 44.89417 on the left and 33.30390 on the right. Both vertical coordinates are 17.04584 px.

The horizontal difference is $d=44.89417-33.30390=11.59027$ px. The point has the same depth $Z$ in both views, so $d=fB/Z$. Moving $Z$ to the other side and dividing by $d$ gives $Z=64\cdot0.8/11.59027\approx4.4175$ m. Pixels cancel, leaving metres. Subtracting the principal point from the left coordinate and restoring the depth scale gives $X=(44.89417-32)\cdot4.4175/64\approx0.89$ m. Vertically, $Y=(17.04584-24)\cdot4.4175/64\approx-0.48$ m. The center has risen, hence the negative sign. Half a second later the second stereo pair gives $(0.89,-0.72,4.2575)$ m. The smaller the disparity, the more a one-pixel mistake matters.

observations = motion.stereo_tracks()
for row in observations:
    (ul, v), (ur, _) = row["left"][-1], row["right"][-1]
    z = motion.FOCAL * motion.BASELINE / (ul - ur)
    xyz = [(ul - 32)*z/64, (v - 24)*z/64, z]
    print(row["t"], "s  XYZ =", np.round(xyz, 5))

## A single rise in place of a pose for every frame

The ribbon has one second to leave its starting position and return. The fraction $r=t/T$ divides elapsed seconds by the duration $T=1$ s. At the beginning $r=0$ and at the end $r=1$. Their product $r(1-r)$ vanishes at each end and reaches $0.5\cdot0.5=0.25$ in the middle. Multiplying by four puts the peak at one. That gives a smooth, dimensionless arc $h=4r(1-r)$.

The canonical center $p_0$ is measured in metres. We add three offsets $a=(a_x,a_y,a_z)$ multiplied by the fraction $h$. The full offset applies halfway through the clip. At a quarter second the fraction is just $4\cdot0.25\cdot0.75=0.75$. Each splat gets its own three offsets.

$$
p(t)=p_0+h(t)\,a.
$$

The orange tip starts at height zero. Its two measured vertical offsets are −0.48 and −0.72 m, both at a height fraction of 0.75. Fitting them separately gives $-0.48/0.75=-0.64$ m and $-0.72/0.75=-0.96$ m. A single arc cannot hit both observations because the recorded ribbon also sways a little. With equal fractions, the midpoint minimizes the sum of squared errors: $(-0.64-0.96)/2=-0.8$ m.

At other times the fractions can differ. For one coordinate, let $d_k$ be the measured displacement and $a$ the amplitude. The index $k$ runs over the observations. The residual between prediction and measurement is $h_k a-d_k$ metres. Squaring each residual and adding them gives the loss. Differentiating the square brings down twice the residual. The slope of the residual with respect to $a$ contributes another factor of $h_k$. The slope at the bottom of this parabola is zero, giving

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \sum_k 2h_k(h_k a-d_k),\\
a\sum_k h_k^2 &= \sum_k h_k d_k,\\
a &= \frac{\sum_k h_k d_k}{\sum_k h_k^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For vertical motion the numerator is $0.75(-0.48)+0.75(-0.72)=-0.9$ m. The denominator is $0.75^2+0.75^2=1.125$ and has no units. Division again gives −0.8 m. With only the first and last instant, both fractions vanish and the denominator is zero. Two frames of the ribbon at rest cannot reveal how high it rose.

model = motion.fit_motion(motion.ribbon(), observations)
print("a =", np.round(model["amplitudes"][-1], 5))
print("t = 0.375 s:", np.round(motion.scene_at(model, .375)["splats"][-1]["center"], 5))

## Three separate checks

First come the left camera and time 0.375 s. The camera is familiar but the time is missing from the observations. Next come the training time 0.25 s and a camera angled at 32°. That tests a different change. The third check combines 0.375 s and 32°. In each row below, frame MSE averages squared errors over $65\cdot49\cdot3=9555$ channel values, with channel intensities from 0 to 1.

For the last splat at 0.375 s, the bend fraction is $h=4\cdot0.375\cdot0.625=0.9375$. Its predicted height is $0-0.8\cdot0.9375=-0.75$ m. The recorded motion puts it at $-0.66515$ m, so the estimate lifts the tip about 8.5 cm too high. At that same time in the unseen view, frame error falls from about 0.007119 for the static ribbon to 0.000364 for the fit. The bright edge on the difference map shows where the mismatch stands out against the background.

print("t        angle   MSE(static)   MSE(fitted)")
for time, angle in [(.375, 0), (.25, 32), (.375, 32)]:
    target = demos.frame(motion.reference_scene(time), angle)
    static = demos.frame(model["canonical"], angle)
    fitted = demos.frame(motion.scene_at(model, time), angle)
    print(f"{time:.3f}    {angle:3}     {np.mean((static-target)**2):.8f}    {np.mean((fitted-target)**2):.8f}")
fig = demos.fit_figure(lang="en")
plt.show()

## What happens between samples

At 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 s, the modeled height of the last splat is −0.6, −0.8 and −0.6 m. Average velocity over the first interval is $(-0.8+0.6)/0.25=-0.8$ m/s. Over the next it is $(-0.6+0.8)/0.25=+0.8$ m/s. The sign flips as the tip turns. A single smooth arc spans the entire second, so there is no jump at a frame boundary. The graph also shows a cost of this assumption. The two black landmarks have different heights, but a symmetric arc always returns the same height a quarter and three quarters of the way through. A motion error can survive even when mean image error is small.

fig = demos.motion_plot(lang="en")
plt.show()

## What goes in the file

Playback needs the rest ribbon, the duration in seconds and five amplitude triplets. Images and landmarks can stay behind. After saving and reloading, the same time and camera should give the same frame. The browser accepts this format in “Motion from JSON”. Opening a custom file puts its canonical scene on the left. Without a reference recording there is no MSE to report.

folder = root / "dynamic-scene-result"
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
path = folder / "lesson-26-en.json"
path.write_text(json.dumps(model, allow_nan=False), encoding="utf8")
restored = motion.validate_model(json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf8")))
np.testing.assert_array_equal(demos.frame(motion.scene_at(restored, .375), 32),
                              demos.frame(motion.scene_at(model, .375), 32))
print(path.name, "·", len(restored["amplitudes"]), "× XYZ")

## A noisy landmark

Suppose the right landmark at 0.25 s moves horizontally by +1 px and the left one stays fixed. Which way will the reconstructed point move? Must the fitted arc pass through it?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

The disparity falls from 11.59027 to 10.59027 px. With the same numerator of 51.2, depth becomes $51.2/10.59027\approx4.835$ m. The point lands about 42 cm behind its original depth of 4.4175 m. The vertical pixel coordinate was unchanged, but converting it to metres now uses the new depth. The arc still has one amplitude per coordinate for two measurements, so it makes a compromise. The noise control introduces alternating positive and negative offsets into the right landmarks, keeping the experiment repeatable.

</details>

title: 27. Where the bytes go

cells.source: The sculpture from lesson 20 fits in a small file. Opening it creates an image. Training it keeps several more arrays alive at the same time. A system monitor will show a very different number. One splat is small enough to count by hand.

## One splat first

Its center has three coordinates measured in meters. Its three widths are positive lengths in meters. Four quaternion components describe orientation. Color has three channels between 0 and 1. Opacity contributes one more number in that range. That makes $3+3+4+3+1=14$ numbers. Float32 assigns 32 bits to each number. A byte has 8 bits, so one number takes $32/8=4$ bytes. One splat takes $14\cdot4=56$ bytes.

The sculpture has 117 splats. The centers alone take $117\cdot3\cdot4=1404$ bytes. All the numeric values take $117\cdot56=6552$ bytes. A binary file adds a header. Text JSON also carries field names, brackets and the digits of decimal numbers. The next cell reads the file and builds the binary packet.

scene, frames = codec.photo_data()
packet = codec.pack_static(scene, 'f32')
print('JSON, bytes:', (codec.ASSETS / 'photo-reference.json').stat().st_size)
print('GSC1, bytes:', len(packet), '= 8 +', len(packet)-8)
print('float32 parameters:', np.empty((117, 14), dtype=np.float32).nbytes)

JSON, bytes: 39038
GSC1, bytes: 6560 = 8 + 6552
float32 parameters: 6552

cells.source:
## When red depends on the view

Constant RGB has one number per channel. In a spherical-harmonic expansion the degree $L$ is a nonnegative integer. Each additional degree adds two more functions than the preceding degree did. Degree zero has one function. Degree one adds three, degree two adds five. Through degree three there are $1+3+5+7=16$ functions. Each needs one coefficient per channel, giving $3\cdot16=48$ color coefficients. These take space before a single pixel is drawn.

The sum of these odd numbers is $(L+1)^2$. At $L=3$ this gives $(3+1)^2=4\cdot4=16$. Let $N$ count the splats. Each splat also has $3+3+4+1=11$ numbers outside color. The parameter total in **bytes** is

$$
B=4N\left(11+3(L+1)^2\right).
$$

For 117 splats at degree three, $4\cdot117\cdot(11+48)=27612$ bytes. The degree control changes the assumed layout. The actual sculpture still uses constant RGB.
display(demos.codec_lab(27, lang))

demos.storage_figure(lang, count=117, degree=0, width=80)
plt.show()

## The screen needs space too

An 80 by 60 frame contains $80\cdot60=4800$ pixels. Three float32 channels take $4800\cdot3\cdot4=57600$ bytes. Adding the sculpture parameters gives $57600+6552=64152$ bytes. In the experiment, height is three quarters of width rounded to the nearest pixel. Doubling both dimensions quadruples the number of pixels.

This count describes specific dense arrays. The course renderer actually returns float64 RGB, with 8 bytes per channel. The cell measures just the array elements with `nbytes`. Python objects, intermediate arrays, projections and libraries also occupy space. A GPU implementation has tile lists and device scratch space. The file length alone cannot tell us their size.

img = render_scene(scene, frames['view-04.jpg']['camera'], 80, 60)
print(img.shape, img.dtype, img.nbytes)
print('float32 copy:', img.astype(np.float32).nbytes)
demos.storage_figure(lang, count=117, degree=3, width=160)
plt.show()

## What training adds

For this count all 14 parameters train in float32. Their gradients take an array of the same shape. Adam keeps a running average of past gradients and a running average of their squares, two more arrays. That makes four equal sets. For the sculpture, $4\cdot6552=26208$ bytes cover **these four arrays**. Other costs depend on the implementation, the visible splats and the values retained for backpropagation. A viewer loading the final scene can discard the gradients and the two running averages.

**Experiment.** With 117 splats, which costs more: raising color degree from zero to three, or adding another 80 × 60 float32 RGB frame?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

The extra coefficients cost $27612-6552=21060$ bytes. The frame takes 57600 bytes. The second buffer costs $57600-21060=36540$ bytes more. At a million splats the balance changes because the frame size stays fixed.

</details>

title: 28. A sculpture in a smaller packet

cells.source: The held-out photograph already reveals the limits of 117 splats. The edges of the sculpture are slightly soft. A smaller file can introduce another kind of error. Both images here share the same camera. The reference is the uncompressed render so that errors from fitting and packing stay separate.

## The first eight bytes

The file begins with four ordinary bytes spelling `GSC1`. The next byte records the bytes per parameter. Another gives the number of color channels. The last two encode the splat count, low byte first. For 117 splats these bytes are 117 and 0 because $117+256\cdot0=117$. The header occupies $4+1+1+2=8$ bytes.

With constant RGB each splat has 14 numbers in this order: center, widths, quaternion, opacity, color. With float32 throughout, the file takes $8+117\cdot14\cdot4=6560$ bytes. Converting the original double-precision numbers to float32 already rounds the least significant digits.

scene, frames = codec.photo_data()
raw = codec.pack_static(scene, 'f32')
print(raw[:8], list(raw[4:8]), len(raw))
decoded = codec.unpack_static(raw)
print('x:', scene['splats'][0]['center'][0], '→', decoded['splats'][0]['center'][0])

## One byte for a coordinate

Suppose $x=1.5$ m falls between $a=1$ and $b=3$ m. The span $b-a$ is 2 m. The fraction of the distance from the left edge is $(1.5-1)/2=0.25$, with the meters cancelling. Eight bits give $2^8=256$ codes, from 0 through 255. There are 255 gaps between them. A fraction of 0.25 lands at $0.25\cdot255=63.75$. The nearest code is 64. On decoding, $64/255\approx0.25098$. Converting back gives $1+2\cdot64/255\approx1.50196$ m, a shift of about two millimeters.

$$
q=\left\lfloor255\frac{x-a}{b-a}+0.5\right\rfloor,\qquad \hat{x}=a+(b-a)\frac{q}{255}.
$$

Here $q$ is the integer code. The floor drops the fractional part after adding one half. The hat on $\hat{x}$ marks a reconstructed value. If the endpoints coincide, code zero decodes to that endpoint. Three coordinates and three widths each need their own pair of bounds. Twelve float32 values add $12\cdot4=48$ bytes. Each component of a normalized quaternion lies between −1 and 1. Color and opacity lie between 0 and 1. Those bounds are already known. The renderer normalizes the decoded quaternion when it converts it to a rotation matrix.

The entire scene now takes $8+48+117\cdot14=1694$ bytes. For a single splat the extra bounds can consume all the savings.
display(demos.codec_lab(28, lang))

demos.static_figure(lang)
plt.show()

## Which splats can go?

Two splats have the same two longest widths, 0.4 and 0.2 m. At opacity 0.8 the first receives a score of $0.8\cdot0.4\cdot0.2=0.064$ square meters. At opacity 0.1 the second scores only 0.008. We retain the larger products. This is a cheap guess at how much image area a splat may influence. It omits camera distance, occlusion and contrast with the background. A tiny bright highlight against a dark surface can disappear. Sorting only decides which splats survive. Their rows stay in the original order.

At a retention of 50%, half of 117 is 58.5. Rounding upward leaves 59 splats and $56+59\cdot14=882$ bytes. Color offers a separate lever. A color such as $(0.9,0.3,0)$ has mean $(0.9+0.3+0)/3=0.4$. The decoder can store that single value and return $(0.4,0.4,0.4)$. This teaching average gives each channel equal weight. One code in place of three saves two bytes per splat, but red and green with the same mean become indistinguishable.

u8-rgb 1694 B; MSE 2.82e-05 frame ms 86.912
