cells.source:
## Reading the comparison

The error maps keep the same scale from 0 to 0.2. Each map pixel is the mean of the three absolute channel differences. The MSE in the title averages their **squares** over every pixel and channel. Timing begins with a warm-up, then uses the median of repeated renders. The browser batches short calls and divides elapsed time by the batch count. Every packet decodes into the same kind of scene. Switching to uint8 does not by itself reduce the number of blends. Removing 58 splats does.

**Experiment.** How many bytes do 59 gray uint8 splats take? What would the same color change save with float32?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

A gray splat has 12 fields, for $56+59\cdot12=764$ bytes. Color used $882-764=118$ more bytes. In float32 the difference would be $59\cdot2\cdot4=472$ bytes. Both changes remove hue.

</details>

title: 29. How much does one second of motion weigh?

cells.source: The colored ribbon from lesson 26 bows to one side and comes back. Its five splats keep their identities throughout. Writing their colors again at every step would repeat the same values. Separating appearance from trajectory lets us see which part of the curve disappears between sparse anchors.

## Seventeen positions, sixteen gaps

The samples cover zero through one second, including both ends. Seventeen samples make sixteen equal gaps of $1/16=0.0625$ s. Five splats have $5\cdot3=15$ coordinates per frame. Four bytes per float32 give $15\cdot4=60$ bytes per frame. One second of centers takes $17\cdot60=1020$ bytes. The binary `GSM1` header adds 16 bytes: four signature bytes, a mode and a reserved byte, three two-byte numbers (frame count, splat count and anchor stride), and four bytes for the residual unit. That makes 1036 bytes.

The packet carries **centers only**, on an evenly spaced timeline. Identity order, fixed shape, color and opacity come from the canonical scene. The duration converts frame indices to seconds. The JSON from lesson 26 already includes that scene, the duration and the motion amplitudes. Its fitted movement is our reference. A player that does not know the original motion law can receive sampled tracks instead. For this particular movement the original formula is especially compact.

model, xyz = codec.motion_data()
packet = codec.pack_motion(xyz, mode='dense')
print('frames × identities × coordinates:', xyz.shape)
print('header + XYZ:', len(packet), 'bytes')
print('duration:', model['duration'], 's')
print('canonical, including starting centers:', len(codec.pack_static(model['canonical'], 'f32')), 'bytes')

## Anchors and the line between them

A stride of eight keeps frames 0, 8 and 16. Three anchors at 60 bytes each plus the header give $16+3\cdot60=196$ bytes. For a coordinate in frame 2, the fraction of the interval from 0 to 8 is $u=(2-0)/(8-0)=0.25$. Suppose the two recorded coordinates are 0.10 and 0.50 m. A quarter of the way across means three quarters of the first value and one quarter of the second:

$$
\hat{x}=(1-u)x_0+u x_8=0.75\cdot0.10+0.25\cdot0.50=0.20\text{ m}.
$$

Each axis of each splat follows the same calculation. The last frame is always an anchor, including when the stride does not divide 16 evenly. A stride of six gives indices 0, 6, 12 and 16. In the final interval the denominator is $16-12=4$ rather than 6. Straight segments save bytes but smooth away curvature. The time control moves both copies together. The camera angle has its own control. The web experiment also accepts a scene JSON from lesson 26.
display(demos.codec_lab(29, lang))

demos.motion_figure(lang, mode='keys', stride=8, time=.37)
plt.show()

## A signed correction

The true coordinate in that frame may have been 0.236 m. The prediction was 0.20 m, leaving a residual $r=0.236-0.20=0.036$ m. Let one code unit mean $s=0.01$ m. In code units the correction is $r/s=3.6$, with nearest integer 4. The decoded coordinate is $0.20+4\cdot0.01=0.24$ m. The remaining error is $0.004$ m. A point below the line has a negative correction.

A signed byte holds integers from −128 through 127. Here the symmetric range −127 through 127 is used. With a 0.01 m unit the largest correction is $127\cdot0.01=1.27$ m. Without saturation, rounding costs at most half a unit. A very small unit narrows the range and large residuals can clip. Anchors need no corrections. The other 14 frames take $14\cdot5\cdot3\cdot1=210$ bytes. With the anchors, that makes $196+210=406$ bytes. Each correction refers to nearby anchors, so an error in one intermediate frame does not propagate to the next.

from deformation import scene_at
from compression_math import pose_with_centers
t, angle = .37, 32
cam = orbit_camera(angle, 55)
reference = render_scene(scene_at(model, t), cam, 65, 49)
for mode in ['dense', 'keys', 'residual']:
    data = codec.pack_motion(xyz, mode, stride=8, quantum=.002)
    track = codec.unpack_motion(data)
    pred = pose_with_centers(model['canonical'], codec.sample_track(track, t))
    error = scores(render_scene(pred, cam, 65, 49), reference)['mse']
    print(mode, len(data), 'B; MSE', round(error, 9),
          'clip decode ms', round(benchmark(lambda: codec.unpack_motion(data)), 4))
demos.motion_figure(lang, mode='residual', stride=8, quantum=.002, time=t, angle=angle)
plt.show()

## A time between frames

A time of 0.37 s maps to frame position $0.37\cdot16=5.92$. Playback mixes decoded frames 5 and 6 with weights 0.08 and 0.92. The fitted model from lesson 26 can evaluate its original curve directly at 0.37 s. Even a file with all 17 samples makes a small error between them. A 32° camera shows how that shift appears from another angle. Here MSE measures disagreement with the original **model motion**, rather than with any training photograph. The timed operation in the table decodes the whole clip. The browser times batches of short calls and divides the elapsed time by the batch length.

**Experiment.** What advantage do residuals retain at an anchor stride of one? How large is the packet?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

All 17 frames become anchors. There are zero intermediate frames, so the corrections take zero bytes. This gives $16+17\cdot60=1036$ bytes, the same size as dense recording. Accuracy between sample times still depends on the sampling frequency.

</details>

title: 30. The final experiment: which scene fits?

cells.source: There is a sculpture, room for 2200 bytes and a viewer drawing at 80 × 60. The largest packet will not fit. The smallest one will, but it may lose color. A short list of measurements, a selection rule and a settings file make the choice repeatable.

## Two photographs with different jobs

First we fix the details that can silently change the outcome. One original model of 117 splats, a white background, the same cameras, an 80 × 60 image and one renderer version. All four packets render `view-00.jpg`. This view helped fit the original sculpture. Here it serves as a calibration image for selecting a compression method. The photograph `view-04.jpg` was held out during training. Its score appears only after the choice. Repeatedly tuning thresholds against that held-out image would call for a fresh camera view for the next independent check.

There are $80\cdot60\cdot3=14400$ channel values. For each one we subtract the target from the prediction, square, sum the differences and divide by 14400. If red is 0.7 instead of 0.6, its contribution is $(0.7-0.6)^2=0.01$. Normalized RGB has a peak channel value of 1. PSNR in decibels is then $10\log_{10}(1/\mathrm{MSE})$. For a mean squared error of 0.01 the ratio is 100. Since $10^2=100$, the logarithm is 2 and the score is 20 dB. Exact agreement gives zero MSE and infinite PSNR.

settings_path = course / 'data' / 'codec-study' / 'settings.json'
cfg = json.loads(settings_path.read_text(encoding='utf8'))
report = codec.benchmark_photo(cfg)
for r in report['candidates']:
    print(f"{r['name']:14} {r['bytes']:5} B   {r['validationPsnr']:.3f} dB   "
          f"decode {r['decodeMs']:.3f} ms   frame {r['renderMs']:.3f} ms")
print(report['selected'], report['test'])

## How four rows become one

| Packet | Contents | Bytes | PSNR on view-00 |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| f32-rgb | 117 float32 splats | 6560 | 20.24 dB |
| u8-rgb | The same 117 in uint8 | 1694 | 20.27 dB |
| u8-half | 59 color splats | 882 | 19.27 dB |
| u8-gray-half | 59 gray splats | 764 | 19.19 dB |

Here PSNR compares each variant **with the photograph**. Rounding can slightly improve an individual pixel in an imperfect original fit. A 0.03 dB difference on one camera says little about the rest of the scene.

The rule is fixed before the comparison. Size must be at most 2200 bytes and quality on the calibration view at least 16 dB. The first packet fails because $6560>2200$. Three remaining packets pass both thresholds. With quality as the priority, `u8-rgb` wins at 20.27 dB. The float32 file would transmit $6560/1694\approx3.87$ times as many bytes. Now the held-out photograph comes into play. Its MSE is about 0.009839, giving $10\log_{10}(1/0.009839)\approx20.07$ dB. Prioritizing size instead would select the 764-byte grayscale packet.
display(demos.codec_lab(30, lang))

demos.study_figure(report, lang)
plt.show()

## Time, memory and the device

Decoding is paid once when the packet opens. Rendering is paid for each new frame. If decoding took 1 ms and each frame took 25 ms, then 40 frames would cost $1+40\cdot25=1001$ ms before network transfer. At 30 frames per second the budget is $1000/30\approx33.3$ ms per frame, including the rest of the application. The latency priority selects the eligible packet with the lowest median render time. Transfer and decode time are separate costs.

A warm-up removes some startup effects. Three measurements of 22, 24 and 61 ms would give a median of 24 ms, the middle observation in sorted order. NumPy on the CPU and JavaScript in a browser are different implementations. The browser times batches of short calls. A float64 RGB output occupies $80\cdot60\cdot3\cdot8=115200$ bytes. That count covers the output array alone. It cannot establish peak process or GPU memory. The [saved report](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/blob/main/data/codec-study/reference.json) records the operating system, architecture and library versions alongside its measured times. Timing deserves a fresh run on another device.

demos.study_figure(report, lang, max_bytes=1000, min_psnr=16, priority='size')
plt.show()
print('80 × 60 × 3 × 8 =', report['candidates'][0]['bufferBytes'], 'bytes')

## What changes for motion?

The sculpture only needs one set of centers. The ribbon from lesson 26 moves. A fair comparison starts with the same canonical packet and adds each motion stream to it. Here that common packet includes the starting centers. Frame rate and clip duration are known to both sides. Transport headers are outside the count.

Suppose there are 500 extra bytes for motion. With five splats, 17 dense frames need 1036 bytes and fail the limit. Anchors every eight frames take 196 bytes, or 406 with residuals. Quality between anchors now matters. The cell uses times 0.19, 0.37 and 0.71 s, none present on the recorded grid. Two cameras see the same motion. First we average the MSE of the six equally sized images and then convert that average error to decibels. This measures compression error against the fitted movement from lesson 26. The sculpture photographs play no part in this comparison.

from deformation import scene_at
model, xyz = codec.motion_data()
base = len(codec.pack_static(model['canonical'], 'f32'))
for mode in ['dense', 'keys', 'residual']:
    packet = codec.pack_motion(xyz, mode, stride=8, quantum=.002)
    track = codec.unpack_motion(packet)
    errors = []
    for t in [.19, .37, .71]:
        decoded = codec.pose_with_centers(model['canonical'], codec.sample_track(track, t))
        for angle in [-25, 32]:
            camera = orbit_camera(angle, 55)
            image = render_scene(decoded, camera, 65, 49)
            target = render_scene(scene_at(model, t), camera, 65, 49)
            errors.append(scores(image, target)['mse'])
    print(mode, 'motion B:', len(packet), 'total B:', base+len(packet),
          'PSNR dB:', round(-10*np.log10(np.mean(errors)), 2),
          'decode ms:', round(benchmark(lambda: codec.unpack_motion(packet)), 4))

## A file for the next run

The [experiment settings](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/blob/main/data/codec-study/settings.json) hold the limits, priority, resolution and repetition count. The Download settings button writes the current values to the same JSON format. The saved file can be opened again in the experiment. From the repository root, the [benchmark script](https://github.com/HeinrichWirth/gaussian-splatting-course/blob/main/scripts/benchmark_codecs.py) reads this file and writes a new report:

```sh
python scripts/benchmark_codecs.py --settings data/codec-study/settings.json --output codec-report.json
```

Byte counts and images follow from the source data and rounding rules. Time is measured on the running machine. Two computers with identical settings can therefore choose different packets when speed has priority.

**Experiment.** Which packet survives a 900-byte limit and a 19.25 dB floor? What changes if the floor rises to 19.5 dB?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

Two packets fit within 900 bytes. The color packet reaches about 19.27 dB and clears 19.25. The gray packet at 19.19 dB falls short. At 19.5 dB all four candidates fail at least one constraint. A larger byte budget or an intermediate retention setting from lesson 28 would open up another experiment.

</details>
